q: A pond freezes from the surface downward each winter, and aquatic life survives beneath the ice layer. Which physical property of water — uniquely tied to its molecular geometry — best explains why solid water (ice) is less dense than liquid water?
opts: High specific heat capacity that buffers temperature changes
Strong cohesive forces and surface tension between water molecules
Water's universal solvent property, which prevents close packing of molecules
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice that spaces molecules apart
The polar O-H bonds, which orient toward charged ions in solution
why: Water molecules form four hydrogen bonds in ice, locking into a tetrahedral hexagonal lattice with empty space between molecules. In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and reform, allowing closer packing — so liquid water is denser than ice. This unusual property allows ice to float and insulate aquatic ecosystems.

q: A biochemist hydrolyzes an unknown polymer and isolates monomers each composed of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. Which class of biological macromolecule did the polymer belong to?
why: Nucleotides — the monomers of DNA and RNA — are composed of a pentose sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), a phosphate group, and one of five nitrogenous bases. Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides, proteins from amino acids, and lipids lack a regular monomer structure.

q: Two glucose molecules combine to form maltose. The reaction releases one molecule of water. This same chemical principle is repeated when many glucose units link to form glycogen or cellulose. What general type of reaction is this?
opts: Hydrolysis, which splits a bond by adding water
Oxidation, with electrons passed to NAD+
why: Polymerization of monosaccharides into disaccharides or polysaccharides is a dehydration synthesis: the OH from one sugar and H from the other combine to form H2O, leaving a glycosidic bond between the sugars. Hydrolysis is the reverse — splitting a polymer with water.

q: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. Cattle and termites overcome this limitation only by harboring symbiotic microbes that produce specific cellulases. What molecular feature accounts for this difference in human digestibility?
opts: Cellulose is built from a different monomer than starch, fructose
Cellulose lacks any glycosidic linkages between its glucose units
Starch is hydrophobic, while cellulose is highly hydrophilic
Cellulose monomers are L-glucose, while starch is built from D-glucose
Starch has α-1,4 bonds; cellulose has β-1,4 bonds we cannot cleave
why: Both polymers are made of D-glucose, but starch uses α-1,4 glycosidic bonds (and α-1,6 branches in amylopectin), which mammalian amylase can hydrolyze. Cellulose uses β-1,4 linkages — the inverted geometry forms tightly hydrogen-bonded fibers that human enzymes cannot cleave.

q: Glucose (an aldohexose) and fructose (a ketohexose) share the molecular formula C6H12O6 but contain their carbonyl groups in different positions and have entirely different overall connectivity. What is the most accurate isomeric relationship between these two sugars?
opts: Stereoisomers, since they differ only in 3D arrangement around chiral centers
Structural (constitutional) isomers, since they differ in atomic connectivity (aldehyde vs ketone)
Diastereomers around a single anomeric carbon
Identical compounds — fructose is just a renamed form of glucose
why: Glucose and fructose share C6H12O6 but differ in connectivity: glucose has the carbonyl at C1 (an aldehyde), fructose at C2 (a ketone). Compounds with the same formula but different connectivity are constitutional (structural) isomers, not stereoisomers.

q: When phospholipids are placed in aqueous buffer, they spontaneously self-assemble into a bilayer in which the phosphate-containing head groups face the water and the fatty-acid tails sequester away from it. Which structural feature drives this organization?
opts: All phospholipid molecules are uniformly hydrophobic
The molecule is amphipathic — a polar phosphate head group and two nonpolar fatty-acid tails
Phospholipids covalently bond to surrounding water molecules to form a network
Their fatty-acid tails carry a partial negative charge that repels water
Phospholipids contain ester bonds that hydrolyze rapidly in water
why: Phospholipids are amphipathic: the phosphate head group is polar and hydrophilic, while the two fatty-acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic. In aqueous solution this dual character drives spontaneous bilayer formation, with hydrophilic heads facing water and hydrophobic tails sequestered inward.

q: Two fatty acids of identical carbon-chain length are isolated from different food sources. Sample A is solid at 25°C (e.g., butter), while sample B is liquid at the same temperature (e.g., olive oil). Which structural difference best explains this physical-state difference?
opts: Sample A contains many cis double bonds, which kink the chain and reduce packing
Sample A is fully saturated, so its straight chains pack tightly
Sample A is polyunsaturated, with at least three C=C bonds per chain
Sample A is phosphorylated at one of its carboxyl carbons
Sample A is composed of D-isomers, while sample B is composed of L-isomers
why: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, allowing straight chains to pack tightly via van der Waals interactions, which raises melting point — they are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fats have cis double bonds that introduce kinks, preventing tight packing, so they remain liquid.

q: Steroid hormones such as testosterone, cortisol, and estradiol all share a four-fused-ring carbon skeleton. They are synthesized in cells from a common precursor lipid that is also a critical component of animal cell membranes. Which lipid is this precursor?
why: Cholesterol is the four-ring sterol that serves as the precursor to all steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone) and bile acids. It is also a key component of animal cell membranes, where it modulates fluidity.

q: An enzyme is incubated at 95°C for 5 minutes. The protein loses all catalytic activity but, when re-analyzed by mass spectrometry, retains its original molecular mass and amino-acid sequence. Which level of protein structure has been preserved despite this denaturation?
opts: Secondary structure — α-helices and β-sheets are stabilized by covalent bonds
Tertiary structure — the 3D fold is held only by covalent disulfide bonds
Primary structure — the covalent peptide-bond sequence is unaffected by heat
Quaternary structure — subunit interactions resist heat better than smaller folds
Both tertiary and quaternary, since only secondary structure is heat-sensitive
why: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids linked by covalent peptide bonds, which require strong proteolytic conditions (not heat) to break. Higher-order structures depend on weaker non-covalent interactions (H-bonds, van der Waals, ionic) that are disrupted by heat — so denaturation destroys 2°/3°/4° but preserves 1°.

q: An α-helix found in keratin is a regular right-handed coil with 3.6 amino-acid residues per turn. The geometry is maintained by repeating non-covalent interactions along the polypeptide backbone. Which interaction primarily stabilizes the α-helix?
opts: Disulfide bridges between cysteine R-groups across the helix
Backbone hydrogen bonds between the amide N-H of residue i and the carbonyl C=O of residue i+4
Ionic salt bridges between charged R-groups (Lys/Arg with Asp/Glu)
Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains in the helix interior
why: The α-helix is stabilized by hydrogen bonds between the backbone amide hydrogen of one residue and the backbone carbonyl oxygen four residues away (i to i+4). R-group interactions can stabilize the overall fold (tertiary structure), but the helix itself is held together by these regular backbone H-bonds.

q: Adult human hemoglobin contains two α-globin polypeptides and two β-globin polypeptides, each with its own folded heme-binding pocket. The four chains assemble into a functional oxygen-transport protein. Which level of protein structure does this multi-subunit assembly represent?
opts: Primary — the linear amino acid sequence of one chain
Secondary — repeating α-helix and β-sheet motifs within each subunit
Tertiary — the 3D fold of a single polypeptide chain
Quaternary — the assembly of two or more separately folded polypeptide subunits
why: Quaternary structure refers to the spatial arrangement of multiple separately folded polypeptide chains (subunits) into a functional protein complex. Hemoglobin's α2β2 architecture is the textbook example. Tertiary structure describes the fold of just one chain.

q: An mRNA strand contains the sequence 5'-AUGCAU-3'. During reverse transcription using the same mRNA as template, the resulting DNA strand is synthesized as the complement. Which nitrogenous base in the RNA template will pair with adenine on the new DNA strand?
opts: Thymine (T) — the standard DNA-DNA pairing partner of adenine
Guanine (G) — pairs with cytosine via three H-bonds
Cytosine (C) — pairs with guanine, never with adenine
Inosine (I) — a modified base in tRNA wobble pairing
Uracil (U) — used in RNA in place of thymine
why: RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. So when adenine on a new DNA strand pairs with the RNA template, the template base is uracil. (DNA-DNA pairing always uses thymine; RNA introduces uracil.)

q: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is hydrolyzed to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate during energy-consuming cellular processes. Considering ATP as a representative nucleotide, what three components are present in every nucleotide?
opts: A pentose (five-carbon) sugar, one or more phosphate groups, and a nitrogenous base
A hexose sugar, an amino group, and a nitrogenous base
Glycerol, one fatty acid, and a phosphate group (as in phospholipids)
An amino acid, a carboxyl group, and a nitrogenous base
A pentose sugar, an aldehyde group, and a hydroxyl base
why: Every nucleotide consists of three components: a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA/ATP, deoxyribose in DNA), one or more phosphate groups attached to the 5' carbon, and a nitrogenous base attached to the 1' carbon. ATP has three phosphates; nucleotides in DNA have one.

q: A pharmacology student measures the kinetics of an enzyme in the presence of inhibitor X. Adding more substrate fully restores the original Vmax, but the apparent Km has doubled. The Lineweaver-Burk plots of inhibited and uninhibited reactions intersect on the y-axis. What kind of inhibitor is X?
why: Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site. Adding more substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so Vmax is unchanged. But the substrate must work harder to reach half-Vmax, so the apparent Km increases. Lineweaver-Burk plots intersect on the y-axis (1/Vmax).

q: Two glucose-binding enzymes are characterized: hexokinase has a Km of 0.1 mM for glucose, while glucokinase (in liver) has a Km of 10 mM. What does the markedly lower Km of hexokinase indicate about its interaction with glucose?
opts: Hexokinase has higher affinity for glucose, reaching half-Vmax at lower [glucose]
Hexokinase is a slower enzyme, taking longer per catalytic cycle
Hexokinase has lower affinity for glucose, needing more substrate to reach half-Vmax
Hexokinase has a higher Vmax than glucokinase under all conditions
Km tells you nothing about substrate-enzyme affinity, only the enzyme's stability
why: Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half-Vmax. A LOW Km means the enzyme reaches that rate at low [S] — high affinity for substrate. Hexokinase's Km of 0.1 mM means it works efficiently at low blood glucose; glucokinase only kicks in at high glucose levels (post-meal).

q: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen in roughly 10^-7 seconds — about a million times faster than the uncatalyzed reaction. Despite this dramatic acceleration, the equilibrium constant of the reaction is unchanged. Which statement best describes how catalase (and enzymes generally) achieves this?
opts: Enzymes raise the activation energy and increase ΔG of the reaction
Enzymes shift the equilibrium toward products by changing ΔG°
Enzymes lower the activation energy without changing ΔG° or K
Enzymes are consumed during the reaction and must be replaced
Enzymes increase the temperature, accelerating molecular collisions
why: Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering the activation energy (Ea), making the transition state more accessible. They do not change ΔG° (which depends only on initial and final states), so equilibrium and Keq are unaffected. Enzymes are not consumed and can catalyze many reaction cycles.

q: A microscopist examines two cell types and finds that one has a clearly defined membrane-bound nucleus while the other has DNA distributed in a region called the nucleoid but lacks any internal compartmentalization. Which of the following is uniquely characteristic of EUKARYOTIC cells but absent in PROKARYOTIC cells?
opts: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
A membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
A plasma membrane separating cytoplasm from environment
DNA used as the hereditary genetic material
Cytoplasm containing dissolved proteins and metabolites
why: Both eukaryotes and prokaryotes have ribosomes, plasma membranes, DNA, and cytoplasm. The defining hallmark of eukaryotes is internal compartmentalization — DNA is sequestered in a membrane-bound nucleus, and other reactions occur in mitochondria, ER, and Golgi. Prokaryotes have neither.

q: Streptomycin is a clinical antibiotic that binds the smaller ribosomal subunit of bacterial ribosomes and disrupts translation, but does not affect host (human) cytoplasmic ribosomes at therapeutic doses. Which Svedberg-coefficient ribosome configuration is found in PROKARYOTES?
opts: 80S total, composed of 60S large + 40S small subunits
70S total, composed of 50S large + 30S small subunits
Membrane-bound ribosomes attached only to the rough ER
Ribosomes made entirely of protein, with no rRNA
why: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S large + 30S small subunits). Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S). Antibiotics like streptomycin and tetracycline exploit this size/structure difference to selectively target bacterial translation while sparing host cells.

q: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes that are similar to those of bacteria. Mitochondria also divide independently of the cell by binary fission, and their double membrane is consistent with engulfment by an ancestral eukaryotic cell. These observations together provide the strongest evidence for which evolutionary theory?
opts: The fluid-mosaic model of membrane structure
Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment
The cell theory (all life is composed of cells)
The chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis
The endosymbiotic theory of eukaryotic origins
why: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria (and chloroplasts) originated when an ancestral eukaryote engulfed a free-living aerobic bacterium. Their bacterial-like (70S) ribosomes, circular DNA, double membrane, and binary fission all support this origin. Cell theory and Mendel's laws address other levels of biology.

q: A pancreatic β cell is secreting insulin. The newly translated insulin precursor passes through the rough ER, undergoes proper folding, and arrives in the next organelle for final modification — including glycosylation, sulfation, and sorting into transport vesicles destined for the plasma membrane. Which organelle handles this final processing and sorting step?
why: The Golgi apparatus is the final processing and sorting hub for secreted proteins. It modifies proteins (glycosylation, sulfation, phosphorylation), packages them into transport vesicles, and directs vesicles to their destinations (plasma membrane, lysosomes, etc.). The rough ER handles initial synthesis and folding.

q: A hepatologist examines liver biopsies from two patients. Patient A is a chronic alcohol user; patient B has no history of substance use. Compared to patient B, patient A's hepatocytes show dramatic enlargement of one organelle that contains the cytochrome P450 family of enzymes. Which organelle is enlarged?
opts: Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes that make proteins
Nucleolus, which expands during ribosome biosynthesis
Lysosome, the site of intracellular hydrolytic digestion
Mitochondrion, where most of the cell's ATP is generated
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a site of lipid synthesis
why: Smooth ER is the site of lipid biosynthesis and drug/toxin detoxification via the cytochrome P450 enzyme system. Chronic alcohol exposure induces hepatocyte smooth-ER expansion (and corresponding tolerance) as the cell upregulates its detoxification machinery. Rough ER (with ribosomes) handles protein synthesis.

q: A specialized organelle within the cell maintains an internal pH of about 4.5 and contains over 40 different hydrolytic enzymes (proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases) that function optimally at acidic pH. These enzymes break down cellular debris, damaged organelles, and engulfed bacteria. Which organelle is being described?
opts: Mitochondrion — site of oxidative phosphorylation at pH ~7
Peroxisome — handles fatty-acid β-oxidation and hydrogen-peroxide breakdown
Lysosome — acidic compartment containing hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion
Golgi apparatus — modifies and packages secreted proteins
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum — site of lipid synthesis and detoxification
why: Lysosomes are acidic (pH ~4.5) compartments full of acid hydrolases that digest cellular debris, damaged organelles (autophagy), and phagocytosed material. The acidic pH is maintained by V-type H+-ATPase pumps and is essential for the enzymes' activity — neutralizing the lumen inactivates them, an autoprotective feature.

q: A medical technologist places a fresh sample of human red blood cells into a 5% NaCl solution (markedly hypertonic compared to plasma's 0.9% saline) and observes them under a microscope after 30 seconds. Which morphological change is expected?
opts: The cells swell and lyse, releasing hemoglobin into the surrounding medium
The cells remain morphologically unchanged, since RBCs are insensitive to ionic concentration
The cells actively pump in NaCl to equalize osmotic pressure
The cells undergo apoptosis, with characteristic membrane blebbing
The cells shrink and develop a crenated appearance as water flows out by osmosis
why: RBCs in a hypertonic solution lose water by osmosis (water flows from low solute → high solute), causing the cells to shrink and develop a wrinkled, spiky appearance called crenation. In a hypotonic solution, the opposite occurs — cells swell and may lyse (hemolysis).

q: A neuron expends roughly 70% of its ATP budget maintaining a steep electrochemical gradient across its plasma membrane: 3 Na+ ions are pumped out and 2 K+ ions are pumped in for each ATP hydrolyzed. Which transport process is being described — and which is the only one that DIRECTLY requires ATP?
opts: Simple diffusion of Na+ and K+ down their concentration gradients
Facilitated diffusion of Na+ and K+ through a gated co-transporter
Osmosis driven by the difference in water concentration
Endocytosis of Na+ and K+ ions packaged in transport vesicles
why: The Na+/K+-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump) is a primary active transporter that directly couples ATP hydrolysis to ion movement against electrochemical gradients (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP). Simple/facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive (no ATP). Secondary active transport uses gradients, not ATP directly.

q: Glucose enters most human cells via GLUT family transporters. The transporter binds glucose on the outside, undergoes a conformational change, and releases glucose on the inside, all without consuming ATP. Glucose movement always proceeds down its concentration gradient. Which transport mechanism is this?
opts: Primary active transport, since a membrane protein moves the glucose
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein
Osmosis, since water follows glucose across the membrane
Endocytosis, with glucose engulfed in a membrane-bound vesicle
Secondary active transport powered by the Na+ gradient
why: GLUT transporters use facilitated diffusion: a membrane protein provides a hydrophilic channel for glucose to cross down its gradient, with no ATP involvement. (SGLT transporters in intestine and kidney use secondary active transport — they couple glucose to the Na+ gradient — but GLUT is purely passive.)

q: Cortisol, a steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex, has its principal physiological effects through changes in gene expression in target cells. Unlike peptide hormones, cortisol passes through the plasma membrane, binds an intracellular receptor, and the receptor-hormone complex translocates to the nucleus. Which mechanism BEST describes cortisol signaling?
opts: Binding to a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) on the cell surface, activating cAMP
Activation of a receptor tyrosine kinase that autophosphorylates
Diffusion across the lipid bilayer, binding an intracellular nuclear receptor, then directly modulating gene transcription as a transcription factor
Opening a ligand-gated ion channel to depolarize the cell
Binding cell-surface integrins and triggering cytoskeletal rearrangement
why: Steroid hormones (cortisol, estrogen, testosterone) are lipophilic and cross the plasma membrane unaided. They bind intracellular nuclear receptors (sometimes after binding cytoplasmic carriers), and the hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, binding response elements in DNA to alter gene expression. Peptide hormones use cell-surface receptors (GPCRs, RTKs).

q: Epinephrine binds to β-adrenergic receptors (a class of G-protein-coupled receptor) on cardiac muscle. The activated Gαs subunit then activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to a small intracellular signaling molecule that activates protein kinase A. Which second messenger does adenylyl cyclase produce?
opts: NADH — the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide
Acetyl-CoA — the entry molecule into the citric acid cycle
Pyruvate — the end product of glycolysis
Cyclic AMP (cAMP), generated from ATP by adenylyl cyclase
Phosphoinositide PIP2, hydrolyzed by phospholipase C
why: GPCRs coupled to Gαs activate adenylyl cyclase, which cyclizes ATP into cAMP. cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates downstream targets to amplify the original hormone signal. (PIP2 → IP3/DAG is a separate Gαq pathway; NADH and acetyl-CoA are metabolic intermediates, not signaling messengers.)

q: Glycolysis converts one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate through 10 enzymatic steps in the cytoplasm. Two ATP are invested early (priming) and four ATP are produced later (payoff), along with reduction of two NAD+ to NADH. What is the NET yield from one glucose molecule entering glycolysis?
opts: 4 ATP and 2 NADH (gross production, ignoring the 2 ATP investment)
4 ATP, 4 NADH, and 4 pyruvate, since glycolysis duplicates
36 ATP per glucose, including downstream oxidative phosphorylation
why: Glycolysis: 2 ATP invested in priming, 4 ATP produced in payoff = NET 2 ATP. Two NAD+ reduced to 2 NADH. One glucose → 2 pyruvate. The 36-38 ATP figure includes all of cellular respiration (Krebs + ETC), not glycolysis alone.

q: Glycolysis is regulated at three irreversible steps. The most heavily regulated of these is allosterically inhibited by high ATP and citrate, and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Which enzyme catalyzes this rate-limiting step?
opts: Hexokinase, which phosphorylates glucose at the entry of glycolysis
Pyruvate kinase, which generates ATP at the final step of glycolysis
Aldolase, which cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two trioses
why: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting (committed) step of glycolysis. It is allosterically inhibited by ATP and citrate (signs of high cellular energy) and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (signs of low energy or high glucose). Hexokinase is regulated more weakly (by product inhibition); pyruvate kinase is the third regulated step.

q: In aerobic cellular respiration, electrons donated by NADH and FADH2 flow through a series of protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (the electron transport chain). After moving through Complexes I-IV, the electrons are passed to a final acceptor that is reduced to water. Which molecule is this final electron acceptor?
opts: Molecular oxygen (O2), reduced to water at Complex IV
NAD+ — recycled back into the citric acid cycle
FAD — recycled back to Complex II
Pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis
Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), which shuttles electrons between Complexes
why: Molecular oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor of the ETC. At Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), oxygen accepts four electrons and four protons to form 2 H2O. This is why aerobic respiration requires oxygen — without it, the ETC backs up, NADH/FADH2 cannot be reoxidized, and oxidative phosphorylation halts.

q: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The acetyl group then enters a cyclic series of eight reactions that generate NADH, FADH2, GTP, and CO2. Where in the mitochondrion does this Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
opts: Outer mitochondrial membrane, which is freely permeable to small molecules
Intermembrane space, where the proton gradient accumulates during ETC flow
Mitochondrial matrix, the compartment enclosed by the inner membrane
Inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae), which houses the ETC complexes
Cytoplasm, in association with mitochondrial outer membrane proteins
why: The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix — the soluble fluid inside the inner membrane. The ETC complexes and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner membrane (cristae); pumped protons accumulate in the intermembrane space; and glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

q: Mitochondrial ATP synthase is a rotary enzyme embedded in the inner membrane. Protons flow through its membrane-spanning F0 ring from the intermembrane space back to the matrix, driving rotation that mechanically catalyzes ATP formation in the F1 head. Where does ATP synthase get the energy to make ATP?
opts: Direct hydrolysis of glucose at the active site
Electrons released from β-oxidation of fatty acids
The proton gradient (pH and electrical potential) across the inner mitochondrial membrane — chemiosmosis
Substrate-level phosphorylation in the matrix using GTP
Direct coupling to the Krebs cycle's reactions
why: ATP synthase uses chemiosmosis: the proton gradient established by Complexes I, III, and IV of the ETC drives protons back through the enzyme. Their flow provides the energy to phosphorylate ADP. Substrate-level phosphorylation (in glycolysis and Krebs) is a separate, smaller source of ATP that does not involve the gradient.

q: An isotopic labeling experiment uses water containing the heavy oxygen isotope (H2-18O) instead of normal water. Plants are grown in this labeled water and the gas they release is collected and analyzed. The released O2 contains the heavy isotope, demonstrating which step of photosynthesis?
opts: O2 originates from water, which Photosystem II splits
O2 originates from the carbon dioxide (CO2) consumed by the plant
O2 originates from glucose breakdown during respiration
O2 originates from NADPH oxidation in the Calvin cycle
O2 is a byproduct of cytochrome b6f activity in the thylakoid membrane
why: The classic experiments of Ruben and Kamen showed that the O2 released by photosynthesis comes from water, not CO2. Photosystem II uses light energy to oxidize water (photolysis), producing electrons, protons, and O2 as a waste product. Carbon from CO2 ends up in glucose, not in O2.

q: The light-independent reactions of photosynthesis (the Calvin cycle) fix CO2 into a 3-carbon sugar precursor (G3P) using ATP and NADPH that were generated by the light-dependent reactions. Where in the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
opts: Thylakoid membrane, where pigment-protein complexes capture light
Thylakoid lumen, where the proton gradient accumulates
Outer chloroplast membrane, in contact with the cytosol
Stroma, the soluble fluid surrounding the thylakoids
Inner chloroplast membrane, the boundary of the stroma
why: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma — the soluble compartment outside the thylakoids. RuBisCO and the other Calvin enzymes are dissolved here. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane (electron transport) and lumen (proton accumulation), analogous to the mitochondrial cristae and intermembrane space.

q: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis use absorbed light energy to drive water splitting and electron transport, which generates a proton gradient and reduces a coenzyme. The two products that are passed to the Calvin cycle to power CO2 fixation are:
opts: Glucose and oxygen, the final outputs of photosynthesis
NADH and FADH2, the same as the mitochondrial inputs to the ETC
CO2 and H2O, supplied by atmospheric exchange
Pyruvate and acetyl-CoA, intermediates of carbon fixation
why: Light reactions output ATP (made by chloroplast ATP synthase using the proton gradient) and NADPH (formed when NADP+ is reduced at PSI). Both fuel the Calvin cycle: ATP provides phosphorylation energy, NADPH provides reducing power for CO2 fixation. NADH and FADH2 are mitochondrial coenzymes, not chloroplast products.

q: During mitosis, sister chromatids — the two identical copies of each replicated chromosome held together at the centromere — are pulled apart and travel to opposite poles of the cell. Which phase is defined by this separation event?
why: Anaphase is defined by the separation of sister chromatids. Cohesin proteins are cleaved by separase (activated when the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied), allowing kinetochore microtubules to pull each chromatid to opposite poles. Metaphase is alignment; telophase is nucleus reformation.

q: A geneticist labels newly synthesized DNA with a thymidine analog (BrdU) in cycling cells. Cells exposed to BrdU only during a brief 1-hour window incorporate the label only if they happen to be in a specific phase of the cell cycle during that window. In which phase does DNA replication take place?
why: DNA replication occurs only in S phase ('synthesis'). Each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. G1 is preparation, G2 is final checks, M is the actual division. BrdU is incorporated only during S, making it a classic S-phase marker.

q: A primary cell-cycle checkpoint integrates extracellular growth signals, nutrient availability, cell size, and DNA damage. If conditions are unfavorable, the cell exits the cycle and enters G0 rather than committing to DNA synthesis. Which checkpoint is this?
opts: Spindle assembly checkpoint, monitoring kinetochore attachment
M-phase metaphase-anaphase transition, monitoring chromatid separation
Cytokinesis checkpoint, monitoring contractile ring formation
G1/S restriction point, where the cell commits to replication
S-phase damage checkpoint, monitoring stalled replication forks
why: The G1/S checkpoint (also called the restriction point) is the major decision: enough nutrients, growth factors, and intact DNA → enter S and commit to DNA synthesis; otherwise the cell enters G0. Loss of this checkpoint (e.g., loss of Rb tumor suppressor) is a hallmark of many cancers.

q: DNA polymerase III in E. coli adds new nucleotides to a growing strand by attacking the 3' OH of the strand's terminal nucleotide and forming a phosphodiester bond with the next dNTP. As a result, the new strand grows in only one direction. In which direction does DNA polymerase synthesize?
opts: It depends on leading versus lagging strand
why: All known DNA polymerases synthesize exclusively 5' → 3' — they catalyze nucleophilic attack of the 3' OH on the α-phosphate of the incoming dNTP. This forces antiparallel synthesis: one strand is made continuously (leading), the other discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (lagging).

q: Before DNA polymerase can begin synthesizing a new strand, the parental double helix must be opened to expose single-stranded templates. Which enzyme uses ATP to break the hydrogen bonds between the two strands and unwind the helix at the replication fork?
why: Helicase is the unwinding enzyme — it uses ATP hydrolysis to break the H-bonds between base pairs and separate the two strands. Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork (a different problem), primase makes RNA primers, ligase seals nicks, and SSB proteins stabilize the exposed single strands.

q: Because DNA polymerase synthesizes only 5' → 3' but the two strands of DNA are antiparallel, replication of the lagging strand proceeds discontinuously. Short DNA segments are synthesized away from the fork, each starting from an RNA primer. These segments are later joined into a continuous lagging strand. What are these segments called?
opts: RNA primers, which remain in the final product
Replication errors caused by polymerase slippage
Okazaki fragments of new lagging-strand DNA
Telomeric repeats added by the enzyme telomerase
why: Okazaki fragments are the short DNA segments (1-2 kb in eukaryotes) synthesized on the lagging strand. Each starts from an RNA primer made by primase, is extended by DNA polymerase, then has its primer removed and is ligated to the next fragment. The leading strand is synthesized continuously.

q: Eukaryotic mRNA is transcribed and processed in one cellular compartment, then exported across the nuclear envelope to be translated into protein in another compartment. In contrast to prokaryotes, this physical separation prevents simultaneous transcription and translation. Where in a eukaryotic cell does TRANSCRIPTION occur?
opts: In the cytoplasm, where ribosomes are also located
On free ribosomes throughout the cytoplasm
On the rough endoplasmic reticulum, near membrane-bound ribosomes
In the mitochondrion only, since that is where the DNA is kept
In the nucleus, where RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA
why: Transcription occurs in the nucleus in eukaryotes. RNA polymerase II reads the DNA template and produces pre-mRNA, which is then capped, spliced, and polyadenylated before export to the cytoplasm for translation. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, so transcription and translation can be coupled.

q: After RNA polymerase II finishes transcribing a eukaryotic gene, the resulting pre-mRNA undergoes three major processing steps before nuclear export: addition of a modified guanine residue at the front, addition of a long string of adenines at the back, and removal of intronic sequences. Which of these is added at the 5' end of the pre-mRNA?
why: The 5' cap is a 7-methylguanosine added co-transcriptionally to the first nucleotide of the pre-mRNA via a 5'-5' triphosphate bridge. The cap protects mRNA from 5' exonucleases and is recognized by the ribosomal initiation complex. The poly(A) tail goes on the 3' end; introns are spliced out internally.

q: Translation of an mRNA continues until the ribosome encounters a codon that does not code for any amino acid. Release factors then bind, hydrolyze the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA, and the ribosome dissociates. Which mRNA codons trigger this termination?
opts: AUG only, the universal start codon
UAA, UAG, and UGA — the three stop (nonsense) codons
GCC and GCA, codons for alanine
UUC and UUU, codons for phenylalanine
CGU, CGC, CGA, and CGG — codons for arginine
why: The three stop codons UAA, UAG, and UGA do not code for any amino acid. Release factors recognize them, terminate translation, and release the polypeptide. AUG is the start codon (also codes for methionine internally); the other listed codons code for specific amino acids.

q: During translational elongation, an aminoacyl-tRNA delivers its amino acid to the ribosome. The tRNA enters the ribosome at one specific binding site, then moves through two more sites before being ejected. At which site does an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA FIRST bind?
opts: P site (peptidyl), which holds the growing chain
E site (exit), which releases deacylated tRNAs
A site (aminoacyl), where the next codon is read
M site, an additional regulatory binding site
I site (initiator), used only by the first tRNA
why: Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs first bind the A site, where they pair with the next mRNA codon. Peptide-bond formation transfers the polypeptide to the new amino acid, and translocation moves the tRNA from A → P, while the previous P-site tRNA shifts to E for ejection.

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, an electric field is applied across the gel and DNA migrates through the porous matrix. Because DNA's phosphate backbone is uniformly negatively charged at physiological pH, all fragments migrate in the same direction toward one electrode. Toward which electrode does DNA migrate?
opts: Toward the positive anode, since the phosphate backbone is negatively charged
Toward the negatively charged cathode, since DNA carries positive sugar groups
DNA does not migrate in agarose gels; only proteins move through the matrix
Direction is randomized by molecular tumbling within the gel pores
Toward whichever electrode is at the lower temperature during the run
why: DNA's phosphate groups give it a uniform negative charge per unit length. In an electric field, negatively charged molecules migrate toward the positive electrode (anode). Smaller fragments encounter less resistance in the gel matrix and travel farther per unit time, separating fragments by size.

q: PCR amplifies a specific DNA segment by cycling a reaction mixture (template, primers, dNTPs, Taq polymerase, buffer) through three temperatures. Each step has a specific role: separating the strands, annealing primers, and extending new DNA. Which sequence of approximate temperatures correctly describes one PCR cycle?
opts: All three steps performed at 72°C with varying durations
why: PCR cycles: ~95°C separates the DNA strands (denaturation), ~50-60°C lets primers bind their target sequences (annealing), and ~72°C is the optimal temperature for Taq DNA polymerase to extend the primers (extension). The use of a thermostable polymerase (Taq, from Thermus aquaticus) is what makes repeated heating possible.

q: A cell biologist wants to visualize the internal architecture of a mitochondrion at a resolution sufficient to count individual cristae and resolve ribosomes within the matrix. Which microscopy technique provides the highest resolution for visualizing INTERNAL ultrastructure of a sectioned organelle?
opts: Light (compound) microscopy, limited to about 200 nm resolution
Fluorescence microscopy, which localizes tagged molecules in cells
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of ultrathin sections
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), which images specimen surfaces
Phase contrast microscopy, which shows living cells without stain
why: TEM passes a beam of electrons through ultrathin sections and is the best technique for resolving INTERNAL ultrastructure (cristae, ribosomes, membranes) at sub-nanometer resolution. SEM scans a surface and shows topology of intact specimens. Light/fluorescence/phase-contrast are all limited by the diffraction limit of visible light (~200 nm).

q: A molecular biologist wants to confirm that a particular mRNA species is being expressed at high levels in liver but not in muscle. They size-fractionate total RNA from each tissue on a gel, transfer it to a membrane, and probe with a labeled cDNA complementary to their mRNA of interest. Which type of blot is this?
why: Northern blot detects RNA: gel separation of RNA, transfer to a membrane, and hybridization with a labeled complementary nucleic-acid probe. Southern blot is the same protocol but for DNA; Western blot uses antibodies to detect proteins. Mnemonic: Southern (DNA) → Northern (RNA) → Western (protein).

q: Restriction enzymes such as EcoRI, BamHI, and HindIII are used in molecular cloning to cut DNA at predictable, sequence-specific locations. EcoRI, for example, cuts at the sequence 5'-GAATTC-3'/3'-CTTAAG-5'. What general type of recognition sequence do most restriction enzymes recognize?
opts: Random sites with no sequence specificity at all
Palindromic sequences that read the same on both strands
Methylated bases that mark host DNA as distinct from foreign DNA
Only GC-rich repeat regions found near gene promoters
Telomeric (TTAGGG) repeats at the ends of chromosomes
why: Most type II restriction enzymes recognize palindromic sequences (e.g., GAATTC on one strand, CTTAAG on the other — same 5' → 3' on both). This palindromic geometry lets the enzyme bind and cut both strands symmetrically. Bacteria use methylation of their own DNA as the strategy to protect themselves from their own restriction enzymes.

q: Coastal regions experience smaller daily temperature swings than inland areas at the same latitude. Marine biologists attribute this thermal stability partly to a unique physical property of liquid water that resists temperature change relative to most other substances. Which property is responsible?
opts: High specific heat, so much heat shifts its temperature only a little
Density anomaly that causes ice to float and insulate the liquid below
Polarity that makes water a nearly universal solvent
Surface tension caused by hydrogen bonding at the air-water interface
why: Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity (~4.18 J/g·°C) — much higher than most substances — because energy must first break extensive hydrogen-bonding networks before raising kinetic energy. Large bodies of water buffer temperature swings, moderating climate near coasts.

q: A 30-meter redwood pulls water from its roots up to its highest leaves through narrow xylem vessels. The water column rises against gravity in a continuous, unbroken stream. Which combination of properties allows this capillary movement to occur?
opts: Gravity, which pulls water passively against pressure gradients
Cohesion (water-water attraction via H-bonds) plus adhesion (water sticking to xylem walls), forming a continuous tension-driven column
Active ATP-driven transport in xylem cells
Osmosis alone, without any cohesive forces between water molecules
Tonic transport via aquaporins in the cell wall
why: Capillary action depends on cohesion (water molecules H-bond to each other) and adhesion (water H-bonds to polar xylem-wall surfaces). As water evaporates from leaves, the tension pulls the entire water column upward — the cohesion-tension theory of plant transport.

q: When ranking common intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest among biological systems, four major types are typically considered: ion-dipole, hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole, and London dispersion forces. Which is the STRONGEST of these intermolecular forces?
opts: Hydrogen bond (a strong dipole-dipole between H attached to N/O/F and another N/O/F)
London dispersion (instantaneous fluctuations in electron density)
Ion-dipole, which involves a full ionic charge interacting with a dipole
Dipole-dipole, between permanent dipoles in neutral molecules
Van der Waals (a synonym for London dispersion forces)
why: Among intermolecular forces, ion-dipole is strongest because a full ionic charge generates much stronger electrostatic attraction with a dipole than mere partial charges do. The order from strongest to weakest: ion-ion > ion-dipole > H-bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion.

q: A peptide bond between two amino acids in a polypeptide is a covalent linkage formed by dehydration synthesis. To cleave this bond and recover the two free amino acids, an enzyme must drive the reverse reaction. What does hydrolysis of a peptide bond require?
opts: Release of one water molecule, the same as in dehydration synthesis
Addition of one water molecule across the C-N bond
Neither addition nor release of water; it is a purely thermal cleavage
Removal of one CO₂ molecule, similar to a decarboxylation
Addition of one molecule of NH₃ across the C-N bond
why: Hydrolysis is the reverse of dehydration synthesis: a water molecule is split across the C-N peptide bond, regenerating a free carboxyl on one amino acid and a free amino on the other. Proteases (e.g., trypsin) catalyze this in proteins; lysosomal hydrolases do this in cells.

q: Mammals store glucose primarily as glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscle. Glycogen is a highly branched polymer with α-1,4 linkages along chains and α-1,6 linkages at branch points (every 8-10 residues). The branched structure is functionally important because it maximizes:
opts: Many non-reducing ends, so phosphorylase can release glucose fast
Maximum carbon storage density per unit volume of cytoplasm
Insolubility, so glycogen does not osmotically disrupt the cell
Sweetness, since a branched glucose polymer tastes more sugary
Resistance to amylase, preventing digestion of glycogen in the gut
why: Branching multiplies the number of non-reducing ends — the substrate sites for glycogen phosphorylase. Many phosphorylase molecules can act simultaneously, mobilizing glucose-1-phosphate rapidly during fight-or-flight or fasting. Linear starch (less branched) mobilizes more slowly.

q: An adult who experiences abdominal cramps, bloating, and diarrhea after consuming dairy products produces normal levels of pancreatic enzymes but lacks one specific brush-border enzyme. As a result, lactose passes undigested into the colon, where bacterial fermentation produces gas. Which enzyme is deficient?
opts: Sucrase, which hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose + fructose
Maltase, which hydrolyzes maltose into two glucose molecules
α-amylase, which cleaves starch into maltose and dextrins
Lactase, which hydrolyzes lactose into glucose + galactose
Trypsin, a pancreatic protease unrelated to carbohydrates
why: Lactase (β-galactosidase) cleaves the β-1,4 glycosidic bond between galactose and glucose in lactose. In lactose intolerance, lactase production declines after weaning (most adults worldwide are lactase-deficient). Undigested lactose passes to colonic bacteria, which ferment it producing the symptoms.

q: Trans fats are produced industrially by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils. Despite containing C=C double bonds (as do cis-unsaturated fats), trans fats behave more like saturated fats: they are solid at room temperature and raise LDL cholesterol. Which structural feature explains this similarity?
opts: Trans fats have no C=C double bonds remaining after partial hydrogenation
Trans bonds are stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding to neighboring chains
Trans fats are more highly branched than cis fats, so they stack in layers
Trans fats contain charged groups that cause the chains to aggregate
The trans geometry keeps the chain straight, so the chains pack tightly
why: Cis double bonds bend the chain by ~30°, preventing tight packing — these fats stay liquid (oils). Trans double bonds keep the chain nearly straight (like a saturated bond), so the molecules pack like saturated fats: solid at room temperature, harder to digest, and associated with elevated LDL.

q: Animal cell membranes maintain consistent fluidity across a wide temperature range. At high temperatures, the membrane resists becoming too fluid; at low temperatures, it resists becoming too rigid. One specific lipid component sits between phospholipids and contributes both effects. Which lipid is this?
opts: Cholesterol, which buffers fluidity at both temperature extremes
Glycoprotein, which provides cell-cell recognition at the surface
Free fatty acid, the building block of stored triglycerides
Sphingomyelin, a phospholipid found primarily in lipid rafts
why: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipids and acts as a fluidity buffer: at high temperatures it restrains lipid movement (less fluid), at low temperatures it disrupts ordered packing (more fluid). Without cholesterol, animal membranes would solidify in cold or melt in heat.

q: Disulfide bonds are critical to the tertiary structure of many extracellular proteins (e.g., insulin, antibodies). They form by oxidation of two thiol (-SH) side chains, creating a covalent S-S bridge. Between which two amino-acid residues do disulfide bonds form?
opts: Two cysteine residues, whose -SH groups oxidize to an S-S bridge
Two methionine residues (which contain a thioether, not a thiol)
One cysteine and one methionine, joined through sulfur atoms
Two serine residues, whose -OH groups condense to an O-O bond
Cysteine and selenocysteine, a rare selenium-containing residue
why: Only cysteine has a thiol (-SH) side chain that can oxidize to form a covalent disulfide (-S-S-) with another cysteine. Methionine has a thioether (-S-CH3) that cannot. Disulfide bonds form most readily in oxidizing environments (extracellular space, ER lumen) and stabilize tertiary/quaternary structure.

q: β-pleated sheets, the second major secondary-structure element after the α-helix, consist of two or more strands of polypeptide running side by side (parallel or antiparallel). The strands are held together by regular non-covalent interactions between backbone atoms. Which interaction stabilizes the β-sheet?
opts: Disulfide bridges between cysteines on adjacent strands
R-group ionic bonds between oppositely charged side chains
Hydrophobic clustering of nonpolar side chains across strands
Aromatic π-stacking between phenylalanine side chains
Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups
why: β-sheets are stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds running across strands — the carbonyl C=O of one polypeptide's backbone H-bonds with the amide N-H of the adjacent strand. R-groups can fine-tune stability but the structural framework is backbone H-bonding (analogous to α-helices but laid out side-by-side rather than coiled).

q: When a globular protein folds in aqueous solution, the polypeptide adopts the conformation that minimizes free energy. The hydrophobic effect — driven primarily by the entropy of surrounding water molecules — is one of the largest energetic contributions to folding. As a result, hydrophobic R-groups in a folded protein tend to:
opts: Face outward toward water, where they form van der Waals contacts with surrounding solvent
Form hydrogen bonds with water and remain solvent-exposed
Become charged (deprotonated) to gain solubility in water
Cluster in the protein's interior, away from water — the hydrophobic core
Distribute randomly throughout the protein with no preference
why: Hydrophobic R-groups (Val, Leu, Ile, Phe, Met) cluster in the protein's interior. Burying them releases ordered water molecules that had been forming clathrate-like structures around them — a large entropy gain. Polar/charged R-groups remain on the surface to interact with water.

q: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic β-cells in response to elevated blood glucose. It consists of two short polypeptide chains (A: 21 residues, B: 30 residues) linked by disulfide bonds. After binding its membrane receptor (a receptor tyrosine kinase), insulin triggers GLUT4 mobilization. To which class of hormone does insulin belong?
opts: Steroid hormone made from cholesterol (e.g., cortisol)
Amine hormone derived from tyrosine (e.g., epinephrine)
Peptide hormone, cut from a polypeptide precursor
Eicosanoid made from arachidonic acid (e.g., prostaglandin)
Thyroid hormone, an iodinated tyrosine derivative
why: Insulin is a 51-amino-acid peptide hormone, processed from preproinsulin → proinsulin → mature insulin. Like other peptide hormones, it cannot cross the lipid bilayer and binds cell-surface receptors (insulin receptor is an RTK), triggering intracellular signaling. Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic and cross membranes.

q: Nitrogenous bases fall into two structural families: pyrimidines, with a single six-membered ring, and purines, with a fused six- and five-membered ring system. Which of the following is a PURINE?
opts: Cytosine, found in both DNA and RNA
Uracil, which replaces thymine in RNA
Orotate, a precursor made on the way to UMP
why: Purines (Adenine and Guanine) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil) have one ring. Mnemonic: 'Pure As Gold' (purines = A, G); 'CUT the Py' (pyrimidines = C, U, T). The size mismatch is why purine-pyrimidine pairing keeps the DNA helix uniform in width.

q: X-ray crystallography of B-form DNA shows the double helix has a remarkably uniform diameter (~2 nm) along its entire length, regardless of sequence. This uniformity is essential because polymerases and other proteins must track along DNA without sequence-dependent obstacles. What structural rule maintains this constant width?
opts: All four bases happen to have the same physical dimensions
Each base pair is composed of one purine (two-ring, ~3 Å wider) paired with one pyrimidine (one-ring), giving a uniform total width
Hydrogen bonds between bases all have identical lengths
The pentose sugars on opposite strands are slightly different
Stacking interactions force any base size into the same width
why: Watson-Crick pairing always pairs a two-ring purine (A or G) with a one-ring pyrimidine (T or C). Purine + pyrimidine = same total dimension every base pair, giving the helix uniform width. Pyrimidine-pyrimidine pairings would be too narrow; purine-purine too wide.

q: When DNA is heated, the two strands separate (denature) at a temperature called the melting temperature (Tm). DNA samples enriched in G-C base pairs have noticeably higher Tm values than samples enriched in A-T pairs. What is the structural reason?
opts: G-C pairs are physically shorter and thus harder to separate by stretching
G-C pairs are typically located at chromosome ends, where they are protected
G-C pairs are heavily methylated, and the methyl groups stabilize them
G-C pairs use covalent bonds, while A-T pairs are non-covalent
G-C pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds, while A-T pairs form only 2
why: G pairs with C using three hydrogen bonds (N-H...O, N-H...N, N-H...O), while A pairs with T using only two (N-H...O, N...H-N). More hydrogen bonds = more energy required to break = higher Tm. GC-rich genomes (e.g., thermophilic bacteria) are correspondingly more thermostable.

q: RNA differs from DNA in three key ways: it is typically single-stranded, it uses uracil instead of thymine, and its sugar (ribose) carries an extra 2'-hydroxyl group. The 2'-OH has direct chemical consequences for RNA's stability and reactivity. Which is the most important consequence?
opts: RNA is more chemically stable than DNA, allowing long-term storage
The 2'-OH gives RNA a permanent positive charge at cellular pH
RNA is less stable: its 2'-OH can cleave the nearby phosphodiester
RNA molecules are larger than DNA molecules of the same length
The 2'-OH allows RNA to bind directly to membrane lipids
why: The 2'-OH on ribose can act as an intramolecular nucleophile, attacking the adjacent 3'-phosphate and cleaving the phosphodiester backbone — especially at alkaline pH or with metal ions. This is why RNA is hydrolytically less stable than DNA, supporting RNA's role as a transient information molecule rather than a permanent genetic store.

q: An enzyme inhibitor reduces the apparent Vmax in a Michaelis-Menten kinetic assay but leaves Km unchanged. Adding more substrate cannot fully restore Vmax. The Lineweaver-Burk plots intersect on the x-axis. Where on the enzyme does this inhibitor bind?
opts: The active site, competing directly with substrate (competitive inhibitor)
An allosteric site distinct from the active site, lowering effective enzyme amount regardless of [S] (non-competitive inhibitor)
The substrate molecule itself, sequestering it
The cofactor only, not the enzyme
why: Non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site (away from the active site), distorting the enzyme so it cannot complete catalysis. Adding more substrate cannot rescue Vmax — effectively, some enzyme molecules are 'turned off.' Km is unchanged because the remaining (uninhibited) enzyme has the same substrate affinity.

q: Many enzymes require additional non-protein helpers for activity: metal-ion cofactors such as Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Fe²⁺, and coenzymes. Which statement about coenzymes is most accurate?
opts: Coenzymes are inorganic metal ions such as Zn²⁺ and Mg²⁺
Coenzymes are always proteins, folded like the enzyme itself
Coenzymes are permanently bound to the enzyme and cannot dissociate
Coenzymes are organic molecules, often vitamin-derived (NAD⁺, FAD)
Coenzymes are denatured, inactive forms of the enzyme itself
why: Coenzymes are organic helpers (often vitamin-derived: NAD⁺ from B3, FAD from B2, CoA from B5, biotin from B7). They typically transfer chemical groups or electrons (e.g., NAD⁺/NADH transfers electrons). Cofactors (the broader term) include both inorganic ions AND coenzymes. Some coenzymes are permanently bound (prosthetic groups) but most are not.

q: In bacterial isoleucine biosynthesis, isoleucine itself binds and inhibits the very first enzyme of the pathway (threonine deaminase). When isoleucine levels are high, the entire pathway shuts down; when isoleucine drops, biosynthesis resumes. Which regulatory mechanism is this?
opts: Feedforward activation by the first substrate
Competition between two pathways for a precursor
Hormonal regulation by an outside signal
Random mutation of the pathway genes
why: Feedback inhibition is a classic regulatory motif: the end product of a pathway allosterically inhibits the FIRST committed enzyme. This conserves resources by shutting off the entire pathway when product is sufficient. The Ile-deaminase example is the textbook case (Umbarger, 1956).

q: Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding curve is sigmoidal rather than the hyperbolic shape predicted by Michaelis-Menten kinetics. The same shape is also typical of allosteric enzymes such as aspartate transcarbamoylase. Which property explains the sigmoidal curve?
opts: Hyperbolic Michaelis-Menten kinetics with no special features
Strictly linear (zero-order) kinetics, independent of substrate concentration
Cooperativity: binding at one subunit raises the affinity of the others
No saturation, since allosteric enzymes have an unlimited number of sites
The reaction proceeding in reverse at high substrate concentration
why: Allosteric enzymes (and hemoglobin) have multiple subunits that show cooperativity: binding the first substrate increases affinity at neighboring subunits. The result is a sigmoidal (S-shaped) saturation curve. This makes the protein highly responsive in a narrow concentration range, ideal for switch-like regulation.

q: A small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule that exists separately from the main chromosome and replicates autonomously is found in a microbial genome. The molecule frequently carries antibiotic-resistance genes and can transfer between cells via conjugation. Which kind of organism most commonly carries such DNA elements?
opts: Eukaryotes, where plasmids are commonly found in the nucleus
Archaea only, and never in any bacterial species
Bacteria, where plasmids often carry resistance genes
Mitochondria, which carry plasmids instead of a circular chromosome
Viruses, where plasmids serve as the entire genome
why: Plasmids are extrachromosomal, circular DNA molecules characteristic of bacteria. They replicate autonomously and often carry antibiotic resistance, virulence, or metabolic genes. While yeast (eukaryotes) have plasmids, the textbook association — and the basis for cloning vectors — is bacterial.

q: Two E. coli cells make physical contact via a hollow protein appendage. One cell (donor F+) transfers a copy of its F plasmid through this appendage into the recipient (F−) cell, converting it to F+. This process is the bacterial form of horizontal gene transfer through direct cell-cell contact. Which structure mediates this transfer?
opts: Sex pilus (F pilus), a hollow protein appendage extended from the donor cell
Type III secretion system, used to inject toxins into host cells
why: Conjugation transfers DNA via a sex pilus (F pilus), a hollow protein appendage encoded by the F plasmid that pulls the donor and recipient together and forms a conduit for plasmid transfer. Transformation is uptake of free environmental DNA; transduction uses bacteriophage as a DNA delivery vector.

q: Peroxisomes are small, single-membrane organelles that participate in fatty-acid β-oxidation (especially of very-long-chain fatty acids) and other metabolic reactions. A characteristic byproduct of these reactions is broken down within the peroxisome by an enzyme that gives the organelle its name. What dangerous byproduct is detoxified by peroxisomal catalase?
opts: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), split by catalase into water and O₂
Ammonia (NH₃), which would be detoxified to urea instead
Lactic acid, which is carried to the liver and metabolized
Free radicals such as superoxide, broken down by superoxide dismutase
Hydrochloric acid, neutralized by buffering inside the organelle
why: Peroxisomal oxidations (β-oxidation, amino-acid oxidation) produce hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. Catalase converts 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂, preventing oxidative damage. The organelle's name comes from this reaction. Superoxide is handled by separate SOD enzymes.

q: Animal cells contain a microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) located near the nucleus. During cell division, this structure organizes the mitotic spindle. It contains a pair of perpendicular cylindrical bodies, each composed of nine triplets of microtubules. Where are these centrioles found?
opts: Inside mitochondria, anchored alongside the matrix
Inside the lysosome, where they regulate digestion
Inside the nucleus, attached to the nucleolus
Free in the cytoplasm, with no organizing structure
Within the centrosome, in the cytoplasm
why: Centrioles are paired cylindrical structures in the centrosome — the primary MTOC of animal cells. The centrosome nucleates microtubules and during mitosis duplicates and migrates to opposite poles to organize the spindle. Plant cells have MTOCs but lack discrete centrioles.

q: Highly active cells (e.g., pancreatic acinar cells, lymphocytes) feature a prominent dense substructure visible inside the nucleus. This sub-organelle is the site of synthesis of one specific class of RNA and the assembly of another major cellular machine. What is the function of the nucleolus?
opts: Site of DNA replication during S phase of the cell cycle
Holds transcription factors that regulate mRNA expression
Storage compartment for excess histones before chromatin assembly
Site of mRNA splicing and 5' cap addition to new transcripts
Site of rRNA synthesis and assembly of pre-ribosomal subunits
why: The nucleolus is a dense subnuclear region where RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNA genes and where rRNA is assembled with ribosomal proteins to form pre-ribosomal subunits. These are exported to the cytoplasm for final maturation. Its prominence reflects ribosome demand.

q: Microtubules form the longest and stiffest filaments of the cytoskeleton. They organize the mitotic spindle, serve as tracks for kinesin/dynein motor proteins, and form the core of cilia and flagella. Microtubules are polymers of which protein dimer?
opts: α-tubulin and β-tubulin heterodimers forming hollow tubes
Actin, which polymerizes into thin microfilaments
Keratin, an intermediate filament protein of epithelia
Vimentin, an intermediate filament in mesenchymal cells
Lamin, an intermediate filament forming the nuclear lamina
why: Microtubules are hollow tubes (~25 nm diameter) built from protofilaments of α/β-tubulin heterodimers. They have a polarity (+/- end), bind GTP, and serve as motor protein tracks. Actin → microfilaments (~7 nm); keratin/vimentin/lamin → intermediate filaments (~10 nm).

q: The thinnest filaments of the cytoskeleton (~7 nm in diameter) form a dynamic network beneath the plasma membrane and drive amoeboid cell motility, contraction in muscle (paired with myosin), and the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis. Which protein polymerizes into these filaments?
opts: Actin, whose G-actin monomers polymerize into F-actin
α/β-tubulin, the building block of microtubules
Keratin, an intermediate filament protein of epithelia
Lamin, an intermediate filament of the nuclear lamina
Myosin, a motor protein that walks along the filaments
why: Microfilaments are polymers of actin: G-actin (globular) monomers polymerize into F-actin (filamentous) double helices ~7 nm in diameter. Myosin is the motor protein that walks along actin (e.g., in muscle contraction). Tubulin makes microtubules; keratin/lamin make intermediate filaments.

q: A laboratory technician accidentally places red blood cells into pure distilled water rather than 0.9% saline. Within seconds, the cells visibly swell and many burst, releasing hemoglobin into the surrounding solution. Which osmotic environment caused this and what was the outcome?
opts: Hypertonic environment; water left the cells, which shrank and crenated
Hypotonic environment; water entered the cells until they lysed
Isotonic environment; cells remained morphologically unchanged
Hypertonic environment; cells actively pumped water in to equalize
Cells underwent apoptosis, with characteristic membrane blebbing
why: Distilled water has zero solute (hypotonic relative to RBC cytoplasm). Water flows into the cell down its concentration gradient via osmosis, the cell swells, and the membrane ruptures (hemolysis). Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall, so they cannot resist this swelling — unlike plants or bacteria.

q: Macrophages engulf invading bacteria by extending pseudopodia around them, sealing them inside a membrane vesicle, and merging that vesicle with a lysosome for digestion. The initial engulfment is one form of bulk transport that brings large solid particles INTO the cell. What is this process called?
why: Phagocytosis is a specialized form of endocytosis used by macrophages, neutrophils, and amoeba to engulf large particles (bacteria, dead cells, debris). The pseudopodia surround the target, the membrane closes to form a phagosome, and lysosomes fuse to deliver hydrolytic enzymes for digestion. Pinocytosis handles dissolved solutes.

q: Epithelial cells lining the intestine are joined by specialized intercellular junctions that prevent water and small solutes from leaking between adjacent cells. As a result, all material crossing the epithelium must pass through the cells (transcellular route), allowing tightly regulated absorption. Which junction creates this barrier?
opts: Gap junction, which allows direct passage of small molecules between cells
Desmosome, which anchors cells via intermediate filaments for strength
Tight junction, a claudin and occludin band that seals adjacent cells
Adherens junction, which links the actin filaments of cells via cadherins
Plasmodesmata, channels that cross plant cell walls but not animal cells
why: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are belts of claudin and occludin proteins encircling each cell. They form an impermeable seal between adjacent cells, blocking the paracellular pathway. This forces solutes to cross transcellularly, allowing regulated, polarized absorption (e.g., glucose via apical SGLT, basolateral GLUT).

q: Hormone binding to one G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) on a cell can ultimately activate thousands of downstream protein-kinase A molecules within seconds. The signaling pathway gains enormous amplification at each step. Which mechanism best explains this signal amplification?
opts: Each activated enzyme catalytically makes many copies of the next messenger in the cascade
The original receptor binds the hormone with very high affinity, so binding is nearly permanent
The hormone diffuses back out of the cell and activates more receptors on neighboring cells
Second messengers are permanent and keep accumulating in the cytoplasm without being degraded
The hormone covalently bonds to all of the downstream target proteins at the same time
why: Signaling cascades amplify because each enzyme step is catalytic. One activated GPCR can activate ~100 G proteins, each Gαs activates ~10 adenylyl cyclases, each cyclase makes ~1000 cAMP, etc. Multiplicative amplification across stages turns a single hormone-receptor binding event into a massive intracellular response.

q: Growth-factor binding to a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) like the EGF receptor causes receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation of cytoplasmic tyrosines. Adapter proteins (Grb2-Sos) recruited to phosphorylated tyrosines then activate a small GTPase, which activates a downstream three-tier kinase cascade. What is this cascade?
opts: The Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK MAPK cascade, driving gene transcription
Adenylyl cyclase activation, generating cAMP that activates PKA
Phospholipase C hydrolysis of PIP₂ to IP₃ and DAG
Direct gene transcription by the receptor, which enters the nucleus
JAK-STAT activation, the pathway used by cytokine receptors
why: RTK activation typically triggers the MAPK cascade: Ras (small GTPase activated by Sos) → Raf (a kinase) → MEK (another kinase) → ERK (the terminal MAPK), which translocates to the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors. This pathway drives proliferation; mutations in Ras (e.g., K-RasG12D) are common oncogenic drivers.

q: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex. After diffusing across the plasma membrane of kidney cells, aldosterone binds its receptor; the hormone-receptor complex dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus, where it acts as a transcription factor. Where is this receptor located?
opts: Cell surface, as a G-protein-coupled receptor
Cell surface, as a receptor tyrosine kinase
Inside an ion channel, as its regulatory subunit
Anchored to the mitochondrial outer membrane
why: Steroid hormones (aldosterone, cortisol, estrogen, testosterone) are lipophilic and pass through the plasma membrane. Their receptors are intracellular (cytoplasmic in some cases, nuclear in others). The hormone-receptor complex binds DNA response elements and modulates gene transcription directly — slow but durable effects on cell behavior.

q: Hexokinase catalyzes the very first step of glycolysis: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP. This step is highly exergonic (ΔG ≈ −16.7 kJ/mol) and is considered functionally irreversible under cellular conditions. Why is this step physiologically important?
opts: Because the cell lacks any enzyme that can reverse it
Because it requires two ATPs rather than one per glucose
Because it produces ATP rather than consuming it
Because hexokinase has no allosteric regulation at all
Because it traps glucose in the cell as glucose-6-P
why: Hexokinase is functionally irreversible because the ΔG is large and negative. Phosphorylation also traps glucose: G6P is charged and cannot diffuse out via GLUT transporters, committing the molecule to glycolysis. Cells reverse the step (during gluconeogenesis) using a different enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, present mainly in liver and kidney.

q: During intense exercise, skeletal muscle outpaces oxygen delivery. Glycolysis continues at high rate, producing pyruvate and NADH, but mitochondrial respiration cannot keep up. Lactate fermentation kicks in: pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. What is the primary purpose of this conversion?
opts: To generate additional ATP directly from pyruvate
To produce pyruvate from amino acids during fasting
To convert lactate to glucose by gluconeogenesis
To regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue
To generate CO₂ that buffers the lactic acid in the blood
why: Glycolysis depletes NAD+ rapidly at the GAPDH step (NAD+ → NADH). Without aerobic respiration to reoxidize NADH, glycolysis would halt within seconds. Lactate fermentation regenerates NAD+ by transferring electrons from NADH to pyruvate, allowing glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically.

q: One molecule of glucose enters glycolysis and is converted to 2 molecules of pyruvate. Each pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix, is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, and the acetyl group enters the citric acid cycle. How many TIMES does the Krebs cycle run per glucose molecule?
opts: Once, since one glucose generates one acetyl-CoA
Twice, since one glucose yields two acetyl-CoA
Four times, since each pyruvate runs the cycle twice
It depends on oxygen; the cycle turns more often in low oxygen
Six times, once per carbon atom in glucose
why: Glucose (6 carbons) → 2 pyruvate (3 carbons each) → 2 acetyl-CoA (2 carbons each, releasing 2 CO₂). Each acetyl-CoA enters the cycle once, so the cycle runs TWICE per glucose. Total per glucose: 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP/GTP + 4 CO₂ from the Krebs steps alone.

q: Cyanide poisoning causes rapid cellular death because it binds with high affinity to a specific component of the electron transport chain, preventing electrons from being transferred to molecular oxygen. The result is a complete halt of oxidative phosphorylation. Which complex does cyanide inhibit?
opts: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), inhibited by rotenone instead
Complex III (cytochrome bc1), inhibited by antimycin A instead
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal electron acceptor that transfers electrons to O₂
ATP synthase, which is inhibited by oligomycin
why: Cyanide binds the iron in cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), preventing electrons from reaching molecular oxygen. The whole ETC backs up, ATP production halts, and cells switch to glycolysis (insufficient ATP). Carbon monoxide acts at the same site. Rotenone hits Complex I; antimycin A hits Complex III; oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.

q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a small lipid-soluble molecule that can carry protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the proton gradient established by the ETC. The ETC continues to run (electrons still reach O₂), but ATP synthesis collapses. Excess oxidized NADH energy is released as heat. What is DNP classified as?
opts: An ETC inhibitor that blocks electron flow
An uncoupler — it dissipates the proton gradient, separating (uncoupling) the ETC from ATP synthesis; energy is released as heat instead of chemical bonds
An ATP synthase activator that boosts ATP production
A Krebs-cycle inhibitor that blocks decarboxylation
An NAD+ regenerator that bypasses lactate fermentation
why: DNP (and related uncouplers like FCCP, plus the natural uncoupling protein UCP1 in brown adipose) carry protons across the inner membrane, collapsing the gradient. The ETC keeps oxidizing NADH but ATP synthase has no driving force — energy escapes as heat. Brown fat uses this physiologically for non-shivering thermogenesis.

q: When all major pathways of cellular respiration (glycolysis, pyruvate decarboxylation, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain, oxidative phosphorylation) are accounted for under modern P/O ratio estimates (NADH ~2.5 ATP, FADH₂ ~1.5 ATP), what is the approximate net ATP yield per glucose?
opts: ~10 ATP, comparable to anaerobic glycolysis alone
~30-32 ATP, the modern estimate (older textbooks reported ~36-38 using P/O of 3 and 2)
~50 ATP, if every electron made one ATP
why: Modern estimates: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (cytoplasmic), pyruvate dec. 2 NADH, Krebs 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 GTP per glucose. Using P/O ratios of 2.5 (NADH) and 1.5 (FADH₂), net yield is ~30-32 ATP. Older texts used 3 and 2, giving ~36-38. Cytoplasmic NADH may use the glycerol shuttle (loses 1 ATP each).

q: Photosystem II uses light energy to split water in a unique reaction: 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ + O₂. The electrons replace those that have been excited and passed down the photosynthetic electron transport chain. The protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen, contributing to the proton gradient. What is the principal product released to the atmosphere from this water-splitting step?
opts: O₂ — molecular oxygen, regenerated as a 'waste' product of photolysis
NADPH, the reducing power for the Calvin cycle
Glucose, the end product of photosynthesis
ATP, generated by chloroplast ATP synthase
why: Water photolysis at PSII generates O₂ as a byproduct. This is the source of nearly all atmospheric oxygen. The electrons replace those excited by light at PSII; the protons add to the thylakoid lumen gradient. NADPH is generated downstream (at PSI/ferredoxin/NADP⁺ reductase); ATP is made by chloroplast ATP synthase.

q: The Calvin cycle in chloroplasts fixes CO₂ into a 5-carbon sugar (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, RuBP), forming an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two 3-carbon molecules. The enzyme catalyzing this carboxylation is the most abundant protein on Earth. Which enzyme is it?
why: RuBisCO catalyzes CO₂ fixation onto RuBP — the entry step of the Calvin cycle. It accounts for roughly half of all soluble protein in plant leaves and is considered the most abundant protein on Earth. It also has a side activity (oxygenase, leading to photorespiration), which is why C4 and CAM plants have evolved to minimize this.

q: Hot, sunny climates increase the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO (photorespiration) which wastes carbon and energy. C4 plants such as corn and sugarcane have evolved a specialized anatomy and biochemistry to minimize this. How do C4 plants suppress photorespiration?
opts: By directly inhibiting the oxygenase site of RuBisCO with a small-molecule inhibitor made in the chloroplast
By closing stomata permanently so that O₂ can never enter the leaf mesophyll tissue
By opening their stomata and fixing CO₂ only at night, storing it as malic acid in vacuoles (the CAM strategy)
By fixing CO₂ with PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells, then concentrating it at RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells
By abandoning the Calvin cycle entirely and fixing all of their carbon through glycolysis run in reverse
why: C4 plants use PEP carboxylase (no O₂ side reaction) in mesophyll cells to fix CO₂ into oxaloacetate. This 4-carbon molecule travels to the bundle-sheath cells, where decarboxylation releases CO₂ at high local concentration around RuBisCO. The high CO₂:O₂ ratio suppresses RuBisCO's oxygenase activity, minimizing photorespiration.

q: CAM (crassulacean acid metabolism) plants — typified by cacti and succulents — open their stomata only at night to conserve water in arid environments. They fix CO₂ at night using PEP carboxylase, store the carbon as malate in the vacuole, and release CO₂ into the Calvin cycle during the day. What is the primary advantage of this strategy?
opts: Fixes O₂ instead of CO₂ during the hottest part of the day
Stores additional water in the leaf tissue overnight
Performs anaerobic photosynthesis without an electron transport chain
Doubles its ATP yield per CO₂ fixed compared to C3 plants
Fixes CO₂ at night and stores it, so stomata can close by day
why: CAM plants temporally separate CO₂ uptake (night, stomata open) from carbon fixation (day, stomata closed). Nocturnal CO₂ is fixed by PEP carboxylase to oxaloacetate → malate, stored in vacuoles. During day, malate releases CO₂ to RuBisCO. Closing stomata during hot days dramatically reduces water loss — critical in arid habitats.

q: After DNA replication in S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids held together along their length, with the strongest attachment at the centromere.
