A multiprotein complex physically clamps the sister chromatids together until anaphase, when it is cleaved by separase. Which protein complex is this?
opts: Cohesin, a ring-shaped SMC complex of proteins
The kinetochore, a protein disk at the centromere
Condensin, an SMC complex that compacts chromosomes
Lamins, intermediate filaments of the nuclear lamina
Histone H1, the linker histone between nucleosomes
why: Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex that physically encircles sister chromatids, holding them together from S phase until anaphase. At the metaphase-anaphase transition, the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied and separase cleaves cohesin, allowing sisters to separate. Condensin compacts chromosomes (a separate role).

q: During mitosis, replicated chromosomes (each consisting of two sister chromatids) undergo a precisely orchestrated series of movements directed by the spindle apparatus. There is a specific phase in which all chromosomes are aligned along the equator of the cell, with each centromere attached to spindle fibers from BOTH poles. Which phase is this?
opts: Metaphase, just before the chromatids separate
Prophase, when the nuclear envelope breaks down
Anaphase, when sister chromatids move apart
why: Metaphase is defined by chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate. Each sister chromatid pair attaches to spindle fibers from both poles (bi-orientation). Only when all chromosomes are bi-oriented and tension is sensed does the spindle assembly checkpoint allow progression to anaphase.

q: A transcription factor encoded by the TP53 gene is upregulated in response to DNA damage. It activates downstream genes that arrest the cell cycle (e.g., p21, a CDK inhibitor) or trigger apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired. Mutation of this gene is found in over half of human cancers. By what nickname is this protein known?
opts: A cyclin, a regulatory subunit of CDKs
why: p53 (TP53 protein) is famously called the 'guardian of the genome.' It is activated by DNA damage and other stresses; downstream, it transcribes p21 (a CDK inhibitor that arrests the cell cycle at G1/S) and apoptosis genes (BAX, PUMA). Loss of p53 function is one of the most common alterations in human cancers.

q: Animal cells divide their cytoplasm at the end of mitosis through formation of a contractile ring of actin and myosin that pinches the cell in half (cleavage furrow). Plant cells, surrounded by a rigid cell wall, cannot pinch and instead use a different mechanism. How do plant cells complete cytokinesis?
opts: By forming a cleavage furrow with actin/myosin, identical to animal cells
By assembling a cell plate at the cell equator from vesicles delivered along microtubules; vesicles fuse to form a new cell wall and plasma membrane between daughter cells
By assembling a new spindle that mechanically separates the cytoplasm
By forming a septum from mitochondrial-derived membrane
By extruding excess cytoplasm through a single pore
why: Plant cytokinesis uses a cell plate, not a cleavage furrow. Microtubules deliver Golgi-derived vesicles to the cell equator. Vesicles fuse to form a new plasma membrane and cell wall between the daughter cells. The cell plate grows outward until it fuses with the existing cell wall, completing division.

q: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG in vertebrates) at chromosome ends that shorten slightly with each replication cycle. Cells with long-term proliferative potential maintain telomere length using a specific reverse-transcriptase enzyme that carries its own RNA template. In which cell types is this telomerase enzyme MOST highly expressed?
opts: Differentiated somatic cells in stable, fully matured tissues
Aging tissues whose cells are approaching senescence
Bacteria, which use telomerase to seal circular chromosomes
Red blood cells, which lose their nucleus as they mature
Stem cells, germline cells, and most cancer cells
why: Telomerase is highly expressed in stem cells (for self-renewal), germline cells (transmitting full-length telomeres to offspring), and most cancer cells (~90%, which need to bypass replicative senescence). Most differentiated somatic cells repress telomerase, so telomeres shorten with each division — eventually triggering senescence (Hayflick limit).

q: DNA polymerase III in E. coli has very high fidelity (~1 error per 10⁷ bases) thanks to base-selectivity at the active site PLUS a built-in proofreading function. If a wrong nucleotide is incorporated, the polymerase backs up, removes the misincorporated base, and re-polymerizes. Which catalytic activity drives this proofreading?
opts: 3' → 5' exonuclease activity that excises a mispaired base
5' → 3' exonuclease activity, also used to remove RNA primers
Helicase activity, used to separate the two parental strands
Endonuclease activity, used to introduce double-strand breaks
Reverse transcriptase activity, found only in retroviruses
why: DNA polymerase III has 3' → 5' exonuclease activity in a separate domain. When a wrong base is incorporated, the resulting mispairing distorts the active site; the polymerase moves the 3' end into the exonuclease site, removes the wrong nucleotide, and resumes synthesis. This proofreading lowers the error rate ~100-fold beyond base selectivity alone.

q: DNA replication is bidirectional: at each replication fork, one strand is synthesized continuously (leading strand) while the other is synthesized as short fragments (Okazaki fragments) that are later joined. The reason for this asymmetry is intrinsic to the directionality of DNA polymerase. Why does the lagging strand REQUIRE Okazaki fragments?
opts: A different polymerase that only works in short bursts synthesizes the lagging strand
The lagging strand uses a slower polymerase that must stop and restart repeatedly
There is no primer available for continuous lagging-strand synthesis at the fork
Polymerase works only 5' → 3', and the lagging template runs the opposite way
The lagging strand is built from RNA, not DNA, and must be replaced in pieces
why: DNA polymerase only synthesizes 5' → 3'. At a replication fork, one parental strand has its 3' end pointing toward the fork (leading template, continuous synthesis); the other has its 3' end pointing AWAY from the fork (lagging template). Synthesis of the lagging strand must proceed away from the fork in short bursts, each starting from a primer — the Okazaki fragments — which are later joined by ligase.

q: Eukaryotic cells contain three nuclear RNA polymerases that transcribe distinct classes of genes. One specific polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNAs from protein-coding genes, while the other two transcribe rRNA and tRNA respectively. Which polymerase produces eukaryotic mRNA?
opts: RNA polymerase I — transcribes large rRNA genes (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus
RNA polymerase II — transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA, plus most snRNAs and miRNAs
RNA polymerase III — transcribes tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and small RNAs
DNA polymerase, which copies DNA, not RNA
Mitochondrial RNA polymerase, which only transcribes mitochondrial genes
why: RNA Pol II transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA. Pol I makes large rRNA in the nucleolus; Pol III makes tRNAs and 5S rRNA. The Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) coordinates capping, splicing, and polyadenylation, distinguishing mRNA biogenesis from other RNA classes.

q: Many eukaryotic protein-coding genes contain a conserved sequence rich in adenine and thymine, the TATA box. The TATA-binding protein (TBP, part of TFIID) recognizes it to position RNA polymerase II. Where is the TATA box located relative to the gene?
opts: Within the coding sequence, in the middle of the first exon
In the core promoter, about 25-35 bp upstream of the start site
In the terminator, where transcription stops and RNA is released
Only in the 5' untranslated region of the mature, processed mRNA
In an enhancer thousands of base pairs away from the gene body
why: The TATA box is a core-promoter element ~25 bp upstream of the transcription start site. TBP binds the AT-rich sequence and bends the DNA, recruiting other general transcription factors and RNA Pol II. Not all genes have a TATA box; some use alternative core elements (e.g., TATA-less CpG-island promoters).

q: After RNA polymerase II transcribes a eukaryotic gene, the pre-mRNA contains both protein-coding sequences and intervening non-coding sequences. A large ribonucleoprotein machine recognizes specific sequences at intron-exon boundaries (5' GU and 3' AG splice sites) and removes the non-coding regions, ligating the protein-coding pieces. What does the spliceosome remove?
opts: Introns, the non-coding sequences, leaving the exons joined
Exons, the protein-coding sequences that interrupt regulatory regions
The poly-A tail added to the 3' end of the mRNA
The 5' methylguanosine cap added during transcription
Both exons and introns, removed indiscriminately
why: The spliceosome (a complex of snRNPs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) excises introns and joins exons. Splice sites are marked by GU at the 5' splice site and AG at the 3' splice site. Alternative splicing (using different exon combinations) lets one gene produce multiple protein isoforms — vastly expanding proteome diversity.

q: After eukaryotic transcription terminates, ~150-250 adenine residues are enzymatically added to the 3' end of the pre-mRNA by poly(A) polymerase. This poly(A) tail is bound by poly(A)-binding proteins (PABP) and serves multiple functions in mRNA biology. Which is the PRIMARY function of the poly(A) tail?
opts: Translation initiation by directly binding ribosomes
mRNA stability (protects from 3' exonucleases) and nuclear export, plus enhanced translation efficiency through PABP-eIF4G circularization
Direct ribosome binding through codon-anticodon pairing
Splicing of introns from the pre-mRNA
Encoding the C-terminus of the encoded protein
why: The poly(A) tail protects mRNA from 3' → 5' exonucleases, is required for nuclear export, and enhances translation by recruiting PABP, which interacts with the eIF4G/cap complex to circularize the mRNA — increasing ribosome reinitiation. Tail shortening (deadenylation) is a major signal for mRNA decay.

q: When a small ribosomal subunit scans an mRNA from the 5' cap looking for the start of translation, it identifies a specific codon to initiate protein synthesis. This codon also codes for the first amino acid of every protein (later cleaved in many cases). Which mRNA codon is the universal start codon?
opts: GUG, used as an alternative start in a few bacterial genes
UAA, one of the three stop codons that end translation
AAA, which codes for lysine and is common in poly(A) tails
UUU, which codes for phenylalanine in every organism
AUG, the methionine codon that serves as the start codon
why: AUG is the universal start codon. It pairs with the special initiator tRNA carrying methionine (in eukaryotes) or N-formyl-methionine (in prokaryotes). Some bacteria use GUG as an alternate start, but AUG is dominant. Internal AUGs encode methionine in the elongation phase.

q: The ribosome catalyzes peptide bond formation between the carboxyl end of a growing polypeptide (in the P site) and the amino group of an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA (in the A site). The catalytic activity is NOT performed by a protein but by an RNA molecule. Where in the ribosome does peptide bond formation occur?
opts: By rRNA of the large subunit
By mRNA in the small subunit
By the exit tunnel at the E site
why: The ribosome is a ribozyme. The peptidyl transferase active site in the large subunit is composed entirely of rRNA (no protein side chains involved in catalysis). This was a major piece of evidence for the RNA World hypothesis — that ancient catalysis was RNA-based before proteins took over most enzymatic functions.

q: Crick's wobble hypothesis explains how 61 sense codons can be read by fewer than 61 different tRNA species, because one codon position tolerates non-standard pairing (inosine in a tRNA anticodon can pair with U, C, or A there). Which codon position shows wobble?
opts: 1st codon position (5' end), which is fully redundant across codons
2nd codon position, where U can pair with G in the anticodon
Anticodon center (middle of the tRNA), which has no role in pairing
Both 1st and 2nd positions, but never the 3rd position
3rd codon position, which pairs with the 5' base of the anticodon
why: Wobble occurs at the 3rd codon position, which pairs with the 5' (first) position of the anticodon. Modified bases like inosine here can pair with multiple bases (U, C, A), so one tRNA can recognize several codons coding for the same amino acid. This explains the observed redundancy of the genetic code.

q: When a protein destined for secretion (e.g., insulin, antibody) is being translated, a short hydrophobic sequence near the N-terminus is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP). SRP halts translation and brings the ribosome to a specific organelle, where translation resumes and the polypeptide is threaded into the lumen. Where is the ribosome directed?
opts: Mitochondrion, where signal sequences direct matrix proteins
Cytoplasm, where free ribosomes translate cytosolic proteins
Rough ER, where the polypeptide enters the lumen
why: Signal peptides direct ribosomes to the rough ER. SRP binds the signal sequence as it emerges from the ribosome and brings the complex to the SRP receptor on the ER membrane. The Sec61 translocon then channels the polypeptide co-translationally into the ER lumen, where signal peptidase cleaves the signal peptide. Mitochondrial, nuclear, and peroxisomal proteins use post-translational targeting via different signals.

q: A point mutation is a change at a single nucleotide position in a gene. Depending on which codon and how the resulting protein is affected, the consequence varies dramatically. Which set of outcome categories accurately describes the possible effects of a point mutation in a coding region?
opts: Always silent — no effect because of code redundancy
Silent (no amino-acid change), missense (different amino acid), or nonsense (premature stop codon)
Always frameshift, since one nucleotide alters the reading frame
Always splice-site changes, regardless of codon
why: A single nucleotide substitution can be (a) silent — wobble-position change with no amino-acid change; (b) missense — different amino acid encoded; or (c) nonsense — substitution to a stop codon, truncating the protein. Frameshift mutations result from insertions or deletions, not single substitutions.

q: Sickle-cell disease is caused by a single nucleotide change in the β-globin gene that converts an A to a T at the second codon position. The result is a substitution of glutamate (Glu, GAG) by valine (Val, GTG) at position 6 of the β-globin chain — a single amino-acid change with profound clinical consequences. What type of mutation is this?
opts: Frameshift mutation, shifting the reading frame downstream
Silent mutation, with no amino-acid change
Missense mutation — Glu → Val at β-globin position 6, changing one amino acid
Nonsense mutation, creating a premature stop codon
why: Sickle-cell is the textbook missense mutation. A single A→T substitution changes Glu (acidic, charged) to Val (hydrophobic) at position 6 of β-globin. The resulting hydrophobic surface patch causes hemoglobin to polymerize when deoxygenated, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape — driving anemia, vaso-occlusion, and pain crises.

q: DNA point mutations are categorized into two types based on how the substitution affects the chemical class of the base. One type substitutes within the same chemical family (e.g., A↔G), while the other type swaps between families. Which definition correctly distinguishes these two types?
opts: Transition and transversion are interchangeable terms, with no real distinction between them
Transition: purine to purine or pyrimidine to pyrimidine; transversion: purine to pyrimidine
Transversion: a change that is always silent; transition: a change that is always missense
Both types create stop codons by definition, differing only in the base that is swapped
Transition: a change that affects only RNA; transversion: a change that affects only DNA
why: Transition is a purine→purine or pyrimidine→pyrimidine substitution (chemically similar). Transversion is purine→pyrimidine (or vice versa) — a bigger structural change. Transitions outnumber transversions about 2:1 because they are easier to make (similar ring structure makes mispairing easier during replication).

q: Cells run several DNA repair pathways, each specialized for a different kind of error or damage. One of them identifies the newly synthesized strand just after replication, excises a short patch, and resynthesizes it. Which type of error does mismatch repair primarily fix?
opts: UV-induced thymine dimers, removed by nucleotide excision repair
Double-strand breaks, repaired by homologous recombination
Mispaired bases left behind after replication
DNA methylation marks, which are not damage at all
Interstrand crosslinks between the two complementary strands
why: Mismatch repair targets base-base mispairs and small insertion/deletion loops left after DNA replication. In E. coli, MutS recognizes the mismatch, MutL/MutH cleave the unmethylated (newly synthesized) strand, and a polymerase + ligase complete the repair. Inherited mutations in MMR genes (MSH2, MLH1) cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary colon cancer).

q: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) develop severe sun-induced skin damage and dramatically elevated skin-cancer risk. Their cells are unable to repair UV-induced thymine dimers, which then cause replication errors and mutations. XP is caused by a defect in which DNA repair pathway?
why: Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by mutations in NER genes (XPA-XPG). NER recognizes bulky helix-distorting lesions like UV-induced thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers), excises a ~25-30 nt oligonucleotide containing the lesion, and resynthesizes. Without NER, dimers persist and cause mutations during replication.

q: The lac operon in E. coli contains three structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) for lactose metabolism, plus a regulatory gene encoding a tetrameric protein that binds the operator and blocks transcription in the absence of lactose. Which gene encodes the lac repressor?
opts: lacZ, which encodes β-galactosidase, the enzyme that cleaves lactose
lacY, which encodes lactose permease, importing lactose into the cell
lacI, the regulatory gene that encodes the Lac repressor protein
The CAP-binding site, a regulatory DNA sequence rather than a gene
why: lacI is the regulatory gene encoding the Lac repressor (a tetrameric protein). When lactose is absent, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. When allolactose (an isomer of lactose) is present, it binds the repressor and removes it from DNA, allowing transcription. lacZ, lacY, lacA are the structural genes.

q: The lac operon is positively regulated by catabolite activator protein (CAP, also called CRP), which binds DNA only when complexed with cyclic AMP (cAMP). Glucose levels modulate cAMP via inverse regulation of adenylate cyclase. When does CAP-cAMP bind the lac promoter and activate transcription?
opts: When glucose is high, so plenty of the preferred sugar is available
Glucose levels do not affect CAP function in any way
When glucose is low, so cAMP rises and CAP-cAMP forms
Only when glucose and lactose are at equal concentrations
Only at very high temperature, when the operon is stressed
why: Glucose suppresses cAMP via catabolite repression. When glucose is LOW, cAMP rises, binds CAP, and CAP-cAMP binds the lac promoter to recruit RNA polymerase. This means the lac operon is expressed only when (1) lactose is present (repressor off) AND (2) glucose is low (CAP-cAMP on) — the cell uses glucose first.

q: Histone tail acetylation by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) such as p300/CBP transfers acetyl groups to lysine residues. The chemical effect is to neutralize the positive charge on lysine, weakening the histone-DNA interaction. What is the typical effect of histone acetylation on gene expression?
why: Histone acetylation neutralizes lysine positive charges, weakening histone-DNA interactions and opening chromatin (euchromatin). Acetylated histones are also bound by bromodomain proteins (e.g., BRD4) that recruit transcriptional machinery. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) reverse this and silence genes; HDAC inhibitors are used as anticancer drugs.

q: DNA methylation in mammals primarily targets cytosines within CpG dinucleotides, especially those clustered in 'CpG islands' near gene promoters. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins (e.g., MeCP2) and chromatin remodelers then assemble repressive chromatin structures. What is the typical effect of CpG-island methylation at a gene promoter?
opts: Causes mutation by damaging the DNA backbone
why: CpG-island methylation (5-methylcytosine in promoter regions) silences gene expression. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and other repressors, compacting chromatin. Aberrant promoter hypermethylation silences tumor suppressors in cancer; X-inactivation and genomic imprinting also use this mechanism.

q: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short ~22-nucleotide non-coding RNAs that, after processing, are loaded into the RISC complex and guide the complex to complementary sites typically in the 3' UTR of target mRNAs. By what mechanism do miRNAs regulate gene expression?
opts: By pairing with target mRNAs, causing decay or blocked translation
By methylating cytosines in DNA, causing epigenetic silencing
By acetylating histones at the promoters of target genes
By splicing pre-mRNA into mature mRNA within the nucleus
By directly binding RNA polymerase II and inhibiting transcription
why: miRNAs base-pair with sites in the 3' UTR (or other regions) of target mRNAs. The miRNA-RISC complex either cleaves the target mRNA (if pairing is near-perfect, plant-like) or represses translation and accelerates deadenylation (mammalian, imperfect pairing). One miRNA can target hundreds of mRNAs, so they sit at major regulatory hubs (e.g., let-7, miR-21).

q: A clinical microbiology laboratory uses Gram staining to differentiate two major bacterial groups. Gram-positive bacteria stain purple/violet, while Gram-negative bacteria appear pink after counterstaining. The difference reflects fundamental cell-wall architecture. What is the structural distinction?
opts: Different DNA structure: linear chromosomes in one group, circular chromosomes in the other
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane; Gram-negative: thin wall plus LPS outer membrane
Different ribosome size: 70S ribosomes in one group and 80S ribosomes in the other
Different plasma membrane composition: cholesterol is present in one group's membrane but absent in the other's
Both groups have identical cell walls, but their cytoplasmic pH differs and alters dye binding
why: Gram-positive bacteria have a single thick peptidoglycan cell wall (retains crystal violet → purple). Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer between an inner plasma membrane and an outer membrane containing LPS (lose crystal violet → counterstain pink). LPS is the endotoxin responsible for septic shock; the outer membrane also makes Gram-negative bacteria more antibiotic-resistant.

q: Some bacteria (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) survive harsh environmental conditions by forming highly resistant dormant structures. These structures contain dehydrated cytoplasm, a thick protein coat, and DPA-Ca²⁺ in their core, allowing them to withstand boiling, desiccation, and UV radiation for years. What are these structures called?
opts: Bacterial endospores, dormant forms made inside the cell
Spore-forming protists, released with motile flagella
Eukaryotic seeds, which are multicellular and dormant
Viral particles released from the cell during lytic infection
Capsule polysaccharide layers secreted around growing cells
why: Endospores are formed within the parent cell in response to starvation. The DPA-Ca²⁺ core, multiple protein coats, and dehydrated cytoplasm make endospores extraordinarily resistant — Clostridium botulinum spores survive boiling. Pressure-cooking (autoclaving at 121°C) is required to kill them. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) spreads via these durable spores.

q: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a strikingly conserved internal structure. A cross-section under TEM reveals a characteristic arrangement of microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair, anchored to a basal body. Which microtubule arrangement defines this axoneme?
why: Motile cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets around two central singlets. Dynein motor arms on the doublets generate movement by sliding adjacent doublets relative to one another. Primary (non-motile) cilia have a 9+0 arrangement and serve sensory functions (e.g., Hedgehog signaling).

q: Bacterial flagella propel cells through liquid environments and look superficially similar to eukaryotic flagella. However, their molecular architecture and energy source are fundamentally different. Which statement correctly distinguishes bacterial from eukaryotic flagella?
opts: Both have the same axoneme structure and use the same propulsion mechanism

Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin protein, are hollow filaments anchored to a rotary motor, and are driven by a proton (or sodium) gradient — not ATP. Eukaryotic flagella are 9+2 microtubule axonemes that bend using dynein-driven sliding powered by ATP.
Bacterial flagella are powered by ATP hydrolysis like eukaryotic flagella
Eukaryotic flagella are simpler than bacterial flagella
why: Bacterial flagella are structurally and energetically distinct: they are flagellin polymers anchored to a rotary motor in the cell envelope, powered by the proton motive force (H+ flow drives rotation). Eukaryotic flagella are 9+2 axonemes built from microtubules; dynein motors, fueled by ATP, slide microtubules to generate bending.

q: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipids in animal cell membranes and modulates membrane fluidity in a temperature-dependent manner. At high temperatures it restrains phospholipid movement; at low temperatures it disrupts ordered packing. Which statement best summarizes cholesterol's effect?
opts: Cholesterol always increases fluidity, regardless of temperature
Cholesterol always decreases fluidity, regardless of temperature
Cholesterol buffers fluidity, opposing both extremes
Cholesterol has no measurable effect on membrane fluidity
Cholesterol only affects fluidity in plant cell membranes, not animal
why: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer. At low temperatures, it prevents tight crystalline packing of phospholipids (maintains some fluidity). At high temperatures, it restrains excessive lateral movement (prevents over-fluidization). The net effect: animal membranes maintain similar fluidity over a wider temperature range.

q: Water can cross lipid bilayers slowly by simple diffusion, but in tissues with high water flux — kidney collecting ducts during ADH-induced water reabsorption, for example — the rate is dramatically increased by integral membrane proteins that form selective channels. What are these proteins called?
opts: Aquaporins, selective water channels that exclude ions
Active transport pumps that use ATP to move water across the membrane
Receptor kinases that signal changes in membrane permeability
Cell-surface glycoproteins involved in cell-cell adhesion
Ribosome-associated translocons that thread water through the ER
why: Aquaporins are integral membrane channels that allow water to cross the bilayer rapidly while excluding ions (their selectivity filter rejects charged species). In the kidney, ADH triggers insertion of AQP2 into collecting duct cells, dramatically increasing water reabsorption. The 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored aquaporin discovery.

q: Protein kinases add phosphate groups to specific serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues, often turning a target enzyme on or off. The reverse reaction is catalyzed by a different family of enzymes that physiologically opposes kinase action. Which enzymes remove phosphate groups from proteins?
opts: Acetyltransferases (HATs), which transfer acetyl groups to lysines
Methyltransferases, which add methyl groups to histones and DNA
Glycosyltransferases, which attach sugar chains to proteins
Sumoylation enzymes, which attach SUMO proteins to lysines
Protein phosphatases, which hydrolyze the phosphoester bond
why: Protein phosphatases reverse the action of kinases by hydrolyzing the phosphoester bond. They are equally critical to cellular signaling — kinase activation must be reversible to give the cell a switch rather than a stuck-on state. The major families are Ser/Thr phosphatases (PP1, PP2A, calcineurin) and tyrosine phosphatases (PTP1B, SHP2).

q: Glycolysis produces a small amount of ATP directly via substrate-level phosphorylation, where a high-energy phosphorylated intermediate transfers its phosphate directly to ADP. Two specific glycolytic enzymes carry out this direct ATP-generating step. Which enzymes catalyze substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis?
opts: Hexokinase, which phosphorylates glucose and consumes ATP to do it
Phosphofructokinase-1, which phosphorylates fructose-6-P using ATP
Aldolase, which splits fructose-1,6-bisP into two triose phosphates
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which produces NADH only
Phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, both making ATP
why: Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis happens at two steps: PGK transfers phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, making ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate; pyruvate kinase transfers phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP. Each step happens twice per glucose (once per triose), giving 4 ATP gross output, minus 2 ATP invested earlier = 2 ATP net.

q: Pyruvate produced by glycolysis enters the mitochondrial matrix, where a large multienzyme complex, pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle in a functionally irreversible step. What reaction does PDH catalyze?
opts: Pyruvate → lactate (in the cytoplasm, under anaerobic conditions)
Acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate (catalyzed by citrate synthase)
Pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH
why: PDH catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate is decarboxylated (loses CO₂), the remaining 2-carbon acetyl group is attached to CoA-SH, and NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The reaction is exergonic and irreversible, locking pyruvate carbons into the Krebs cycle. PDH activity is heavily regulated by phosphorylation (PDK inactivates, PDP activates).

q: The citric acid cycle generates ATP (or GTP) directly at one specific step via substrate-level phosphorylation. The high-energy thioester bond in succinyl-CoA is broken, and the released energy drives phosphorylation of GDP (or ADP). Which Krebs enzyme catalyzes this step?
opts: Citrate synthase, which condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate
Succinyl-CoA synthetase, which forms GTP as succinate is released
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which produces NADH and CO₂
Malate dehydrogenase, which oxidizes malate to oxaloacetate
Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting step that releases CO₂
why: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples thioester hydrolysis (succinyl-CoA → succinate + CoA) with phosphorylation of GDP → GTP (or ADP → ATP, in some isoforms). This is the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle. The other ATP from oxidation comes through the ETC after NADH/FADH₂ are reoxidized.

q: After full aerobic catabolism of one glucose molecule (glycolysis + pyruvate decarboxylation + Krebs cycle), the bulk of the ATP is generated in mitochondria as NADH and FADH₂ feed electrons into the ETC, driving chemiosmosis through ATP synthase. Approximately how many ATP per glucose come from this oxidative phosphorylation alone?
opts: About 4 ATP, comparable to the yield of glycolysis alone
About 14 ATP, since only NADH contributes electrons
About 26-28 ATP from oxidative phosphorylation alone
More than 40 ATP per glucose from the ETC by itself
0 ATP, since oxidative phosphorylation does not make ATP
why: Per glucose, oxidative phosphorylation processes: 10 NADH (~2.5 ATP each = ~25) + 2 FADH₂ (~1.5 ATP each = 3) ≈ 26-28 ATP. Substrate-level phosphorylation contributes another ~4 (2 from glycolysis + 2 from Krebs). Total ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with the lion's share from oxidative phosphorylation.

q: Intestinal epithelial cells absorb dietary glucose against its concentration gradient — moving glucose from low-concentration lumen into high-concentration cell interior. They achieve this without directly hydrolyzing ATP at the transporter; instead they exploit the steep Na+ gradient maintained elsewhere by Na+/K+-ATPase. What kind of transport is this?
opts: Secondary active transport via SGLT, driven by the Na+ gradient
Primary active transport, since ATP is being used at the same membrane
Facilitated diffusion through GLUT, with no energy required
Simple diffusion directly across the lipid bilayer
Endocytosis, with glucose engulfed in membrane vesicles
why: SGLT (sodium-glucose cotransporter) uses secondary active transport. It moves glucose against its gradient by coupling movement to the favorable Na+ gradient — Na+ flows down its gradient and 'drags' glucose with it. The Na+ gradient itself is built by primary active transport (Na+/K+-ATPase using ATP) elsewhere on the cell. SGLT inhibitors are antidiabetic drugs (e.g., empagliflozin).

q: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) prevents anaphase from beginning until every chromosome is properly attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles. Until that condition is satisfied, the SAC inhibits a key cell-cycle E3 ubiquitin ligase that would otherwise trigger anaphase by ubiquitinating securin and cyclin B. Which complex does the SAC inhibit?
opts: Cyclin D-CDK4, the kinase that drives progression through G1
p53, the genome guardian that responds to DNA damage
The retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which blocks G1/S progression
ATP synthase, the mitochondrial F0F1 enzyme
why: The SAC inhibits APC/C^Cdc20 until all kinetochores are attached. Once attachment is complete, SAC release allows APC/C to ubiquitinate securin (whose destruction releases active separase, which cleaves cohesin) and cyclin B (mitotic exit). Loss of SAC function (e.g., Mad2 mutations) causes chromosomal instability, a hallmark of cancer.

q: As a replication fork progresses through DNA, helicase unwinding generates positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Without intervention, the accumulating supercoils would block further unwinding. A specific class of enzyme makes transient cuts in DNA, allowing strands to relax, then reseals the cuts. Which enzyme is this?
opts: DNA ligase, which joins Okazaki fragments
DNA polymerase III, which synthesizes new DNA
Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase in bacteria) — relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork by transiently cutting both strands, allowing relaxation, then resealing
Single-strand binding (SSB) protein, which stabilizes unwound DNA
why: Topoisomerases relieve supercoiling. Type II (gyrase in bacteria, topo IV) cuts both DNA strands transiently, passes another duplex through, and reseals. Type I cuts one strand. Quinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) inhibit bacterial gyrase, killing the cell. Topo II inhibitors (etoposide) are anticancer drugs that trap the cleaved intermediate.

q: When a single mRNA is translated by many ribosomes simultaneously — each ribosome at a different stage along the mRNA — the structure looks like beads on a string under EM. This arrangement amplifies protein output per mRNA molecule and is especially prominent in tissues with high biosynthetic demand. What is this structure called?
why: Polysomes are mRNAs simultaneously bound by multiple ribosomes (typically 1 ribosome per ~80 nt of mRNA). They greatly amplify protein output per mRNA. Active translation polysomes appear by EM as beads-on-a-string. Cells under stress disassemble polysomes (e.g., during the integrated stress response or amino acid deprivation).

q: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Vmax represents the maximum rate of a reaction when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate. Doubling the substrate concentration above this point cannot increase the rate. What primarily determines Vmax in a given experiment?
opts: Substrate concentration, since Vmax is reached only at infinite [S]
Total enzyme concentration times the turnover number (kcat)
Temperature only, with no dependence on the amount of enzyme
Km (Michaelis constant), which is the substrate level at Vmax
pH alone, regardless of the amount of enzyme present
why: Vmax = kcat × [E]_total. It depends on total enzyme concentration (more enzyme = more Vmax) and the enzyme's intrinsic turnover number (kcat). It does NOT depend on substrate concentration (as long as Vmax is approached). Increasing temperature can increase kcat to a point but eventually denatures the enzyme; pH affects kcat indirectly through residue protonation.

q: The Lineweaver-Burk plot is a linearization of the Michaelis-Menten equation. It transforms the hyperbolic v vs [S] curve into a straight line, making it easier to estimate Vmax and Km from the intercepts. Which axes does the Lineweaver-Burk plot use?
opts: Velocity v on the y-axis vs substrate concentration [S] on the x-axis (the Michaelis-Menten plot itself)
1/v on the y-axis vs 1/[S] on the x-axis (the double-reciprocal plot); the y-intercept gives 1/Vmax and the x-intercept gives -1/Km
v vs log [S], which is the Hill plot
ΔG vs [S], showing the reaction energetics
why: The Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot graphs 1/v vs 1/[S]. The Michaelis-Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) inverts to 1/v = (Km/Vmax)·(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = -1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax. The double-reciprocal plot is the classic way to identify inhibitor types (competitive, non-competitive, uncompetitive).

q: Lipase enzymes secreted by the pancreas hydrolyze triglycerides in the small intestine. The reaction cleaves the three ester bonds linking fatty-acid tails to the glycerol backbone, freeing the lipid components for absorption. What two product types are released?
opts: Glycerol (a 3-carbon trihydroxy alcohol) plus three fatty acids
Glucose plus fructose, the two sugar products of disaccharide hydrolysis
Amino acids (the products of protein hydrolysis)
why: Lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides into one glycerol + three fatty acids. Bile salts emulsify fats first, increasing surface area for lipase action. The fatty acids and monoglycerides reform into mixed micelles, are absorbed into intestinal cells, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged into chylomicrons for transport via the lymph.

q: Fatty-acid catabolism oxidatively trims two-carbon acetyl-CoA units from the carboxyl end of an activated fatty acyl-CoA molecule. Each cycle generates one FADH₂, one NADH, and one acetyl-CoA. The pathway also requires functional mitochondria. Where does β-oxidation take place?
opts: Endoplasmic reticulum, where fatty-acid synthesis occurs
Lysosome, the site of acid hydrolysis
Smooth ER, where lipid synthesis takes place
why: β-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (and to a smaller extent in peroxisomes, especially for very-long-chain fatty acids). Long-chain fatty acids must enter via the carnitine shuttle (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I/II), since CoA cannot cross the inner membrane. β-oxidation generates the acetyl-CoA that feeds the Krebs cycle, plus NADH/FADH₂ for the ETC.

q: Cholesterol biosynthesis takes place primarily in the liver. The pathway condenses two-carbon units from acetyl-CoA in a series of reactions, eventually forming the four-fused-ring sterol skeleton through the key intermediate squalene. What is the starting material for cholesterol synthesis?
opts: Glucose, directly converted into the four-ring sterol core
Amino acids, especially glycine and serine
Glycerol, derived from triglyceride breakdown in fat tissue
Inorganic carbonate, fixed into carbon chains by the liver
Acetyl-CoA, which condenses to HMG-CoA and then mevalonate
why: Cholesterol is built from acetyl-CoA. Three acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonate (catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step). The mevalonate pathway eventually produces squalene, which cyclizes to lanosterol and then cholesterol. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to lower blood cholesterol — a $30B/year drug class.

q: Skeletal muscle cells contain a specialized form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions at high concentration. When an action potential reaches the muscle fiber, calcium is rapidly released into the cytoplasm to trigger contraction. What is this specialized organelle called?
opts: Mitochondrial reticulum, a network used to store ATP in the muscle fiber
Cisternae, a generic term for the flattened stacks of the ER
T-tubules, which carry the action potential into the fiber
Sarcoplasmic reticulum, the Ca²⁺-storing smooth ER of muscle
Golgi apparatus, modified in muscle to package and secrete Ca²⁺
why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is a muscle-specific smooth ER that stores Ca²⁺ at ~1 mM (cytoplasmic resting [Ca²⁺] is ~100 nM). T-tubules invaginate from the plasma membrane to deliver action potentials deep into the fiber; voltage-sensors there trigger ryanodine receptors on the SR to release Ca²⁺, initiating contraction (excitation-contraction coupling).

q: After S phase but before mitotic anaphase, each duplicated chromosome consists of two identical copies of the DNA, held together by cohesin most strongly at one specialized region. Each copy is referred to as a sister chromatid. How many sister chromatids does one chromosome contain after S phase but before anaphase?
opts: 1 chromatid (single, unreplicated chromosome — the G1 state)
2 sister chromatids, joined at the centromere by cohesin and identical in DNA sequence
Multiple chromatids (more than 2), one per gene
A random number of chromatids depending on cell type
0 chromatids — the chromosome is dissolved at this stage
why: After S-phase replication, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids — identical DNA copies — held together along their length and especially at the centromere by cohesin. The number of chromosomes is unchanged (e.g., 46 in humans), but each now has 2 chromatids = 92 DNA molecules. At anaphase, sisters separate to opposite poles.

q: HIV is a retrovirus whose genome is a single-stranded RNA. After entering a host cell, the virus must convert its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA before it can integrate into the host genome and be transcribed by host machinery. Which viral enzyme catalyzes this RNA → DNA conversion?
opts: Host DNA polymerase, recruited from the nucleus
Reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that the retrovirus brings into the cell as part of its capsid
Host ribosomes, which translate RNA into DNA
An endonuclease that cuts host DNA at random sites
Integrase, which only handles integration of the proviral DNA
why: Retroviruses (HIV, HTLV, etc.) carry reverse transcriptase as a virion protein. Once in the cell, RT copies the RNA genome to DNA (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity), then makes a complementary DNA strand to form double-stranded DNA, which is integrated by the viral integrase. RT's lack of proofreading is what makes HIV mutate so rapidly. Antiretrovirals (zidovudine, tenofovir) target RT.

q: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in HEXA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme β-hexosaminidase A. As a result, the lipid GM2-ganglioside accumulates in lysosomes (especially in neurons), causing developmental regression and early death. What general type of disorder does this represent?
opts: A disease caused by too many lysosomes forming in each cell
A pH imbalance disorder, where lysosomes are no longer acidic
Lysosomal storage disease: a missing hydrolase lets its substrate pile up
A membrane defect causing lysosomes to leak hydrolases into the cytoplasm
A metabolic disease of the mitochondria, unrelated to lysosomes
why: Lysosomal storage diseases (Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Fabry, Niemann-Pick, Hurler) are caused by single-hydrolase deficiencies. The undegraded substrate accumulates inside lysosomes, swelling them and disrupting cell function. Tissues with high turnover of the affected substrate (often neurons, given their lipid-rich membranes) are most affected. Treatments include enzyme replacement therapy and substrate reduction.

q: A virus particle (virion) consists of a nucleic-acid genome (DNA or RNA) packaged inside a protein shell. The shell is built from many copies of a small number of distinct proteins, often arranged with helical or icosahedral symmetry. What is this protein shell composed of?
opts: A lipid bilayer with embedded proteins
Capsid — a shell built from many copies of capsomere proteins (a small number of distinct subunits arranged with regular geometric symmetry)
The viral nucleic acid itself, which doubles as the shell
Carbohydrate residues secreted by the host cell
An RNA-protein hybrid resembling a ribosome
why: Viral capsids are built from capsomere proteins arranged with high symmetry (often helical, like tobacco mosaic virus, or icosahedral, like adenovirus). Some viruses also have a lipid envelope acquired from host membranes (e.g., HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2), but the capsid itself is protein.

q: On a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, a non-competitive inhibitor produces a characteristic graphical signature compared to the uninhibited reaction. Which axis intercept changes for a non-competitive inhibitor?
opts: Same y-intercept, different x-intercept, with the lines meeting on the y-axis
Different y-intercept, same x-intercept, since Vmax falls and Km is unchanged
Both intercepts change, giving parallel lines with an identical slope
Neither intercept changes, because the inhibitor does not alter kinetics
The slope is unchanged but both intercepts shift by the same amount
why: Non-competitive inhibitor: Vmax decreases (so 1/Vmax = y-intercept goes up), Km unchanged (so 1/Km = x-intercept unchanged). Lines intersect on the x-axis. Competitive: Vmax unchanged (same y-intercept), Km increases (different x-intercept). Uncompetitive: both Vmax and Km decrease (parallel lines).

q: Sanger DNA sequencing — the dominant method until next-generation sequencing — uses chain-terminating nucleotide analogs that are incorporated into a growing DNA strand but lack the 3'-OH needed for further extension. The resulting fragments are separated by size to read the sequence. What are these terminator nucleotides called?
opts: Restriction enzymes, which cut at palindromic sequences
Standard dNTPs, which always extend the chain normally
Reverse transcriptase substrates, used only in retroviral biology
Methylated nucleotides, which only modify base pairing
why: Sanger sequencing uses ddNTPs (dideoxynucleotides). They are missing the 3'-OH, so once incorporated by DNA polymerase, no further nucleotide can be added — the chain terminates. Each ddNTP carries a different fluorescent label, and capillary electrophoresis separates fragments by size, reading the sequence base-by-base.

q: A cell biologist wants to separate cellular organelles or molecular complexes that have similar mass but different densities. They layer the lysate on top of a tube containing a continuous gradient of sucrose (from low concentration at top to high at bottom) and centrifuge. Each component migrates to the layer matching its own density. Which centrifugation method is this?
opts: Differential centrifugation, which separates only by mass at fixed density
Density-gradient centrifugation, which separates particles by density
Microcentrifuge spin, used for small-volume sample concentration
Tabletop centrifuge, used for plate-format separations
Rate-zonal centrifugation, which separates by sedimentation rate
why: Density-gradient (isopycnic) centrifugation uses a sucrose, CsCl, or Percoll gradient to separate particles by density. Each particle moves until it reaches the gradient point matching its own density and stops (zero net buoyant force). Differential centrifugation separates by mass (sequential pelleting at increasing speeds), which is a different principle.

q: Many cell-surface proteins are decorated with covalently attached oligosaccharide chains, forming glycoproteins. These sugars project into the extracellular space, where they participate in cell-cell interactions, antigen recognition, and protection from proteases. What is the primary functional role of these glycoproteins on cell surfaces?
opts: Cell-cell recognition, such as blood-group antigens
Direct ATP synthesis at the outer face of the plasma membrane
DNA replication and chromosomal segregation during mitosis
Direct ion transport across the bilayer, as gated channels do
Photosynthetic light absorption by membrane-bound pigments
why: Surface glycoproteins (and glycolipids) form the glycocalyx and serve as cell-cell recognition tags. ABO blood groups are oligosaccharides on RBC glycoproteins. Selectins on leukocytes recognize sugars on endothelial cells. The sugars also protect the protein backbone from proteases and contribute to the immune system's distinction of self from non-self.

q: In Griffith's classic 1928 experiment, harmless R-strain pneumococci became virulent when mixed with heat-killed S-strain bacteria. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty later showed that DNA was the transforming substance. The bacteria had taken up free DNA from their environment and integrated it into their genome. What is this form of horizontal gene transfer called?
opts: Transduction, where DNA is delivered by a bacteriophage
Conjugation, which requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus
Transformation, uptake of free DNA from the environment
Transposition, where mobile DNA jumps within a single genome
why: Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the environment by 'competent' bacterial cells. Some species (e.g., Streptococcus, Bacillus) are naturally competent; others (e.g., E. coli) need artificial induction. Transformation was the basis of Avery-MacLeod-McCarty's identification of DNA as the genetic material in 1944.

q: When a bacteriophage infects one bacterium and accidentally packages a piece of bacterial DNA inside a phage particle, that DNA can be delivered to a new bacterial host upon subsequent infection. The new host integrates the foreign DNA into its genome and acquires new traits. What is this mechanism called?
opts: Conjugation, mediated by a sex pilus
Direct cell-cell contact, like animal cell fusion
Free DNA uptake from the environment (transformation)
why: Transduction is DNA transfer between bacteria via bacteriophage. Generalized transduction: phage accidentally packages random bacterial DNA. Specialized transduction: prophage excises imprecisely and carries adjacent host genes. Transduction is one of three major bacterial gene-transfer mechanisms (transformation, transduction, conjugation).

q: Water (H₂O, MW 18) has a boiling point of 100 °C, while methane (CH₄, MW 16, similar size) boils at −161 °C. Even hydrogen sulfide (H₂S, MW 34, larger) boils at only −60 °C. Why does water have such an unusually high boiling point compared to molecules of similar size?
opts: Larger molecular mass, since water is heavier than methane
Ionic bonds between water molecules, like those in NaCl
Branched molecular structure that resists evaporation
Greater density than other liquids of similar molecular size
Hydrogen bonds between molecules that must break to boil
why: Water's high boiling point reflects its extensive hydrogen-bond network. Each water molecule can form up to four H-bonds with neighbors. Vaporizing water requires breaking enough of these bonds to release individual molecules to the gas phase — far more energy than dispersing methane (no H-bonds) or H₂S (much weaker H-bonds; sulfur is less electronegative).

A researcher arrests a cell at the G2/M checkpoint by inhibiting the activity of CDK1 (Cdc2) using a small molecule. Which of the following events would most likely FAIL to occur after the arrest is reversed and the cell continues into M-phase?
opts: Lamin phosphorylation and nuclear envelope breakdown
Anaphase-promoting complex activation; cyclin B degradation
Sister chromatid alignment at the metaphase plate
why: CDK1/cyclin B activity is required at multiple M-phase steps. APC activation and cyclin B degradation come AFTER metaphase via the SAC; even with restored CDK1, if APC is downstream, the failure mode would manifest there. The other events (lamin phosphorylation, SPB separation, H3 phosphorylation) are direct CDK1 substrates and proceed once CDK1 activity returns.

q: A point mutation in a DNA-coding strand changes 5'-AAA-3' to 5'-AGA-3'. The original codon coded for lysine and the new codon codes for arginine. Which type of mutation is this and what is its likely functional consequence on a protein?
opts: Synonymous mutation; no change because both are basic
Missense mutation; conservative substitution (basic → basic), often functionally tolerated
Nonsense mutation; produces a stop codon early
Silent mutation in the wobble position
why: AAA (Lys) → AGA (Arg) is a missense mutation but conservative — both are positively-charged residues. Side-chain physiochemistry is preserved, so functional consequence is often minimal compared to non-conservative changes (e.g., Lys → Glu).

opts: The ratio matches 9:3:3:1; no deviation is meaningful
Linkage between the two genes; the 9:3:3:1 ratio is distorted because parental combinations are over-represented
Epistasis; the bb genotype is suppressed
Partial dominance; the AB combination shows incomplete penetrance
why: Expected 9:3:3:1 of 800 = 450:150:150:50. Observed 460/152/158/30. The aabb class is 30 (vs expected 50) — significantly fewer. This suggests homozygous-recessive (aabb) is partially lethal, while other classes match expectations.

q: A patient develops severe hypoxia at altitude. Their kidneys respond by increasing erythropoietin (EPO) secretion, which stimulates erythrocyte production. Over weeks, hemoglobin concentration rises and oxygen-carrying capacity increases. Which control system best characterizes this physiological response?
opts: Negative feedback loop with the bone marrow as the effector and red-cell mass as the controlled variable
Positive feedback loop maintained until oxygen normalizes
Direct neural reflex via the vagus nerve
why: Hypoxia → EPO → erythrocyte production → increased oxygen delivery → restoration of oxygen sensing → reduced EPO. This is a classic negative-feedback homeostatic loop, with red-cell mass / oxygen carrying capacity as the controlled variable.

q: A population of finches on an island shows two distinct beak-size morphs (small and large) but no intermediate-sized birds. Selection pressure favors both extremes due to two distinct food sources. Over generations, the intermediate phenotype becomes increasingly rare. This pattern is best classified as:
opts: Directional selection; one extreme is favored
Stabilizing selection; intermediate phenotypes are maintained
Disruptive (diversifying) selection; both extremes are favored, leading to potential speciation
Genetic drift; random loss of intermediate phenotypes
Bottleneck effect from a recent population crash
why: When selection favors BOTH extremes against the intermediate, that's disruptive selection. It can lead to bimodal phenotype distributions and is one mechanism for sympatric speciation.

q: In glycolysis, the conversion of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to two trioses (DHAP and G3P) by aldolase is followed by triose phosphate isomerase converting DHAP to G3P. If a mutation in TPI eliminates its activity entirely, what is the IMMEDIATE biochemical consequence?
opts: DHAP accumulates; only one triose feeds into the lower glycolytic pathway, halving ATP yield per glucose
Glycolysis is unaffected; G3P comes only from the aldolase step
The pentose phosphate pathway compensates by re-routing G6P entirely
why: TPI normally rescues DHAP by converting it into G3P, keeping the pathway funneling both trioses through. Without TPI, DHAP accumulates and only the aldolase-produced G3P proceeds to substrate-level phosphorylation, reducing ATP/glucose yield.

q: A novel pathogen secretes a toxin that specifically inhibits eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF-2) by ADP-ribosylation. Which of the following best describes the immediate cellular consequence in target cells?
opts: Cessation of cytoplasmic protein synthesis at the translocation step (ribosome stalls)
Block of mRNA capping and splicing
Disruption of the nuclear pore complex
why: eEF-2 is required for ribosomal translocation during translation. ADP-ribosylation by toxins like diphtheria toxin renders eEF-2 inactive, halting cytoplasmic protein synthesis at the translocation step. Mitochondrial translation is unaffected.

q: In a community with three trophic levels (producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers), the introduction of a top predator (a tertiary consumer) typically results in:
opts: Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers rebound, producer biomass decreases
Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers also decline, producer biomass INCREASES
No effect; the new predator only eats producers
Loss of primary consumers across the food web
why: Adding a tertiary predator triggers a top-down trophic cascade: the new predator suppresses secondary consumers, which releases primary consumers from predation pressure (primary consumers rebound), and the increased primary-consumer grazing then reduces producer biomass. Option A describes this classic four-level cascade correctly.
